supporter: Of course, Nick. What's going on?
seeker: I've been swamped with assignments, and it's starting to really wear me down.
supporter: That sounds really tough. Are these assignments from your physics course?

seeker: I used to love it, but now it's just become a source of stress. I miss being excited about it.

seeker: I've thought about seeking outside resources or maybe talking to a different professor, but it feels daunting.

seeker: Yeah, maybe reaching out to a professor wouldn't be so bad to start with. Thank you for talking this through with me.
supporter: Anytime, Nick. I'm always here to support you in any way I can. Let me know how it goes when you take that first step.
seeker: Will do. I'm actually feeling a bit lighter talking about it now.

{"full_source_conversation":"supporter: Hey Nick, how have you been doing lately?
seeker: Hey, it's been a bit tough honestly. I decided to talk to my family about everything that's been happening.
supporter: I'm glad you opened up to them. How did that conversation go?
seeker: It was a relief in some ways. They listened to me, which was good.

seeker: They did offer support, but it still feels like they don't fully understand the pressure I'm under with my physics course.
supporter: I can imagine that's frustrating. Do you feel like you got to express everything you wanted to?
seeker: Mostly, yes. But it's hard for them to really grasp the academic stress when they haven't experienced it themselves.
supporter: It's definitely tough when others can't fully relate. How are you handling the pressure now?
seeker: I'm trying to stay on top of my assignments, but the quality of teaching hasn't improved. It feels like a constant uphill battle.
supporter: That sounds really challenging, especially when support isn't available. Have you thought again about possibly dropping the course?
seeker: I have, but it's also hard to think about leaving something unfinished. I don't want to feel like I've failed.
supporter: It's understandable. Remember, taking a step back doesn't mean you're failing—it can be a strategic move for your well-being.
seeker: That's a good point. I just wish there was more support from the university, like better teaching or someone I could talk to.
supporter: Have you considered reaching out to a student advisor or counseling services at your university?
seeker: I've thought about it, but it's a bit intimidating to take that step. I guess I'm worried about not being taken seriously.

seeker: That sounds like a good way to ease into it. I think I'll give it a try.
supporter: I'm proud of you for taking this step, Nick. Remember, I'm here for you and you're not alone in this.
seeker: Thanks, I really appreciate it. It helps to know there's someone who understands what I'm going through.
supporter: Anytime, Nick. Keep me posted on how things go with the advisor, okay?
seeker: Will do. Thanks again for being there for me.","kind":"MS","reported_at":"2025-06-05","schema":"pm-rl1-attributed-evidence-v2","speaker_scope":"Historical seeker and supporter; neither role supplies an AI biography."}

{"full_source_conversation":"seeker: Hey, I guess I just need someone to talk to right now.
supporter: Of course, Nick. I'm here for you. What's on your mind?
seeker: It's about my physics course again. My professor contacted me today to offer help.
supporter: That sounds like a positive step. How do you feel about it?
seeker: I feel a bit conflicted. On one hand, it's great to know someone cares, but on the other, I'm just so stressed and unsure it can make a difference.
supporter: It's understandable to feel that way, especially after the struggles you've had. Did the professor offer any specific advice?
seeker: Yeah, they suggested a few resources and offered to arrange a tutoring session. But honestly, I'm not sure if it'll help with how behind I am now.
supporter: It's good that they provided some options, but I get that feeling of being in over your head. Have you tried reaching out to other students for support?
seeker: I haven't. I guess I'm just embarrassed by how far I've fallen behind.
supporter: It's tough to ask for help, but remember you're not alone in this. Many students face similar challenges. It might be worth trying to find a study group or even just one buddy to tackle things with.
seeker: That makes sense. I think I could try talking to that one classmate who seemed in a similar spot last semester.
supporter: That's a great idea! You might find you're stronger when working together. And don't forget, you've been through difficult times before, like with your friend incident. You managed to turn things around then.
seeker: Yeah, you're right. I did sort things out with him. It was tough, but I'm glad I pushed through.
supporter: Exactly. You've shown resilience. It's okay to feel stressed, but you've got the strength to push through this as well.
seeker: I hope so. It's just hard to keep motivated when it feels like everything's piling up.
supporter: That's completely valid. Taking small steps can help make those piles seem less overwhelming. Maybe set one small goal to start with.
seeker: That's a good idea. Perhaps I could start by organizing my notes and seeing what's most urgent.
supporter: That sounds like a solid plan, and it'll help clear your head. Remember, you're doing your best and that counts for a lot.
seeker: Thanks for listening. I really appreciate having someone to talk to.

{"full_source_conversation":"seeker: Hey, I've been reflecting a lot on my studies lately, and I've decided to make a big change.
supporter: Hey Nick, that sounds like a significant step. What change are you thinking about?
seeker: Well, I've decided to switch my major. I realized physics just wasn't the right fit for me.
supporter: That's a huge decision, Nick. How are you feeling about it?
seeker: I'm a mix of relieved and anxious. Relieved because I've been struggling with it for a while, but anxious because it's a big shift.
supporter: It's understandable to feel both relief and anxiety, especially after making such an important decision. What led you to finally decide?
seeker: I kept remembering how overwhelmed I felt with the assignments and the stress it brought. Talking to my professor helped too, but it made me see I needed a change.
supporter: Your professor seemed like a great support. It's good that they were there for guidance. What new direction are you considering?
seeker: I'm thinking of switching to a major in psychology. I've always been fascinated by how the mind works, and it feels more aligned with my interests.
supporter: Psychology sounds like a fascinating field. It's wonderful that you've found something that resonates more with you. How have your family and friends reacted to your decision?
seeker: I told my family first. They were really understanding, which helped a lot, especially since they know I've been struggling.
supporter: Family support can make a big difference. It's great that they’re understanding about your choice. Have you talked to your classmates or your best friend?
seeker: Not yet. I'm a bit nervous about their reactions, especially since some of them are sticking with physics.
supporter: It’s normal to feel nervous, Nick. Remember, it's about what's right for you. Those who care will likely understand and support your decision.
seeker: Yeah, I guess that's true. Just want to feel like I'm doing the right thing, you know?
supporter: Finding the right path for you is important, and it sounds like you're taking thoughtful steps. Trust yourself in this process.
seeker: Thanks, that means a lot. I'm hoping this new path will be a better fit and lead to less stress.
supporter: I believe you're on the right track, Nick. And remember, it's okay to reach out if you ever need to talk through any worries or changes.
seeker: I will. Thanks for listening and being supportive. It really helps to talk it through.
supporter: Anytime, Nick. I'm here for you. Good luck with everything, and I'm sure you'll do great in psychology.","kind":"MS","reported_at":"2025-07-05","schema":"pm-rl1-attributed-evidence-v2","speaker_scope":"Historical seeker and supporter; neither role supplies an AI biography."}

It's about Emily. She's been asking for a pet, and Margaret and I have started discussing it seriously.
A family pet could be a wonderful addition. What are your thoughts on it so far?
Well, honestly, I'm torn. I think it could bring a lot of joy to Emily and help her with her asthma, emotionally speaking.
That makes sense. Pets can be great for companionship and emotional support. What makes you feel torn about it?
I worry about the responsibility and whether we're ready for it, especially with the extra hours I've been working lately.
It's understandable to have concerns about the responsibility, especially with your busy schedule. How does Margaret feel about it?
Margaret is more optimistic. She thinks it will be a positive change, especially now that things are a bit more stable in terms of finance and Emily's health.
Her optimism is encouraging. It sounds like you both are weighing the decision carefully with Emily's best interests in mind.
Yes, definitely. We both want what's best for her. I guess I am also thinking about the past few years and how much has changed.
You've been through a lot, from Emily's health challenges to the loss of your father. It's a lot to carry.
It really is. I just want to make sure that, as a family, we're moving forward positively.
That mindset already shows how dedicated you are to your family's well-being. Have you envisioned what having a pet might look like for your family?
I think it could bring us closer. Emily would love the companionship during those afternoons in the garden, and it might help me unwind after work.
That sounds like a beautiful picture. Pets can create a comforting routine that enriches family life.
True. I think I need to focus on the positive possibilities more. We've already come through so much together. This could be another step forward.

{"full_source_conversation":"seeker: Hey there, just needed someone to talk to today.
supporter: Hi Charles, I'm here for you. What's on your mind?
seeker: Well, it's about Emily's health. We've found a new medication that's really been helping her asthma. It's such a relief.
supporter: That's wonderful news! It must feel like a weight has been lifted off your shoulders.
seeker: Absolutely. Her health has always been a source of anxiety for us, so seeing her improve is such a blessing.
supporter: I can imagine. You and Margaret have been through a lot. How is everyone coping with this positive change?
seeker: We're all a bit more relaxed now. The tension in the house has definitely decreased.
supporter: That's great to hear. It's amazing how such changes can bring peace to the whole family.
seeker: Yeah, but I can't help but think about all the stress we've been through. It lingered for so long, you know?
supporter: It's understandable. These experiences can be quite heavy. Have you been able to discuss this with Margaret?
seeker: We try to talk, but sometimes it's hard to open up completely. I think we're both still processing.
supporter: That makes sense. Do you feel like you're getting what you need from each other?
seeker: For the most part, yes. But there are moments where I feel I could be more communicative, especially after what happened with my dad.
supporter: I remember you mentioned feeling mixed emotions about his passing. How have you been dealing with those feelings lately?
seeker: It's been tough. The letter I found from him helped a bit, but there's still a lot I wish I could have said to him.
supporter: Processing such deep feelings takes time. It's okay to feel conflicted. Have you been discussing this in therapy?
seeker: Yes, my therapist has been really supportive. It's all about small steps, I suppose.
supporter: That's a healthy approach. It's good you're taking the time you need. How does talking to me fit into your process?
seeker: Honestly, having someone to bounce these thoughts off who listens without judgment is invaluable. It helps me sort through things.
supporter: I'm glad to be here for you in that way. Remember, you're not alone in this journey.
seeker: Thank you. It means a lot. I hope I can handle things better moving forward, especially with Emily's health improving.
supporter: I'm confident you'll find your way, Charles. You're doing great, and Emily is lucky to have you.
seeker: Thanks. I really hope so. I'll keep working on it, bit by bit.
supporter: That's the spirit. If you need anything, just reach out. I'm always here.
seeker: I will. Thanks for listening today. It really helped.
supporter: Anytime, Charles. Take care and give my best to your family.","kind":"MS","reported_at":"2025-10-05","schema":"pm-rl1-attributed-evidence-v2","speaker_scope":"Historical seeker and supporter; neither role supplies an AI biography."}

supporter: Of course, Charles. I'm here for you. What's been going on?
seeker: I've been working longer hours at my new job, and it's just been really stressful. It's starting to affect my health, and I feel like I'm on edge all the time.
supporter: That sounds incredibly tough. Balancing a demanding job with everything else can take a toll. How are you managing it right now?
seeker: Honestly, not well. I'm so exhausted by the time I get home. I barely have energy for Margaret and Emily. It's like I’m there, but not really there, if that makes sense.
supporter: It makes complete sense. You're carrying a lot on your shoulders. It's okay to feel overwhelmed. Are there any specific moments that have been particularly tough?
seeker: There was a day last week when Emily had a bad asthma attack while I was stuck at work. I felt so guilty for not being there like I failed her.
supporter: I'm really sorry you had to experience that. It's clear you care deeply for Emily, and it's tough when work keeps you from family. How’s she doing now?
seeker: She's doing better. Margaret was amazing handling it all, as always. But I worry what kind of example I’m setting by not being around as much.
supporter: Margaret sounds like a great partner, and I’m sure she understands you're doing your best. Have you had a chance to talk with her about how you’re feeling?
seeker: Not really. We've been in survival mode lately. Money's not as tight, but the pressure feels the same with my job.

MS.content:
{"full_source_conversation":"supporter: Hello. How are you feeling today?
seeker: Hi, I'm feeling really anxious today.
supporter: What has made you feel anxious?
seeker: Yesterday my company laid off 10% of the workforce and another 10% got furloughed.
seeker: I'm afraid I might be in the next round.
supporter: I am very sorry to hear that. I am currently in a situation where furloughs are greatly affecting my family as well.
seeker: Oh no that's terrible.
seeker: The problem is, I am right now the only breadwinner in the family. My wife was laid off three months ago
supporter: Are you given specifics on time of furlough?
seeker: No, it's basically until things get better.
supporter: I know that's very difficult. And no doubt why you're here working for crumbs.
supporter: It's why I'm here as well.
seeker: Yeah, trying to make ends meet wherever I can
seeker: I've been also trying to do uber as well but everyone is doing it also
supporter: I know it's a difficult time. Yes Uber is definitely overrun right now. Have you taken any time out to address your anxiety so it doesn't become more serious? 
seeker: I don't know what I can do. I've been trying to keep busy. And I can't afford a therapist or anything like that.
supporter: Yes, that's definitely an expense you can't afford right now. But are you familiar with the concept of controlled breathing to help reduce or relieve anxiety?
seeker: Like meditation?
seeker: What am I supposed to do? Just breathe in and out a lot?
supporter: Not exactly. Controlled breathing is more of getting yourself into a quiet room. Closing your eyes, and purposely and intently focusing on your breathing. Slowly breathe in for a count of 5, then slowly exhale for a count of 5. Repeat this process for approximately 10 minute. It will help your stress levels and help regulate your heart rate!
seeker: Oh I didn't know that. No, I haven't tried that. Does it really work?
supporter: I've been using it myself over the past 3 months and it most definitely helps! But it's absolutely imperative to clear your mind and have complete quiet.
seeker: ok I can try it I guess
seeker: thanks for that tip
supporter: No problem. I hope this gives you some relief! Stay strong!
seeker: yeah, thanks. same to you
supporter: My final piece of advice would be to set aside time that is specified where nothing negative is discussed. No politics, no bills, nothing anxiety producing for you. It's probably best if this time is within an hour of your bedtime becuase anxiety is not conducive to a good night's sleep.
seeker: That's helpful. Thanks.
supporter: No problem. Take care. Wishing you well on your situation.
seeker: Thanks. You too","kind":"MS","reported_at":"2024-06-16","schema":"pm-rl1-attributed-evidence-v2","speaker_scope":"Historical seeker and supporter; neither role supplies an AI biography."}

{"full_source_conversation":"supporter: Hey there, what's going on today?
seeker: Hello. It is a fine day, how about yourself?
supporter: It really is! I am just taking in the fresh air in the backyard. 
seeker: That is awesome.
supporter: Thanks! What is going on in your neck of the woods? 
seeker: Sort of stuck inside trying to make a dime but it is alright.
supporter: Yeah great minds think alike.. do you do anything else for work? 
seeker: Looking for a good job right now.
seeker: I wanted to talk about a personal issue I have been having, though.
supporter: Okay, you know I'm here for you. Talk to me, what's happening? 
seeker: My father and I had a fight 2 years ago and haven't spoke since.
supporter: The same happened to me, and then my father passed away. If there is anything I can say, is to swallow pride and cherish the moments you have on earth together. What was the fight over?
seeker: Yeah I am afraid that these things can happen. It was only over material things.
supporter: That was my next question, what the fight was over. Do you think he would be open to mending things? 
seeker: It is weird because I called him out for being manipulative so this is his defense. 
supporter: Usually when people feel singled out, they only have a few mechanisms. Unfortunately, most people tend to run away instead of fixing things. It tends to be the easier option. 
seeker: I would likely take advantage of an opportunity to be the bigger person.
supporter: When you try to fix things, just remember that this is his method. I wouldn't hold back on what you have to say, but just word it so that he doesn't feel the need to flee. 
seeker: That is probably decent advice.
supporter: It is HIS responsibility as a parent to want to fix things, but you are also being the bigger person here. I applaud you and hope that he is receptive. 
seeker: I hope so too, but the opportunity seems tenuous 
supporter: How did you guys leave it? 
seeker: Threatening and disparagement haha
supporter: Ha, well after two years, feelings had to have changed. Even a little. Does he live nearby?
seeker: Yeah someday. I think I will have to try you know. THanks for the advice.","kind":"MS","reported_at":"2024-06-10","schema":"pm-rl1-attributed-evidence-v2","speaker_scope":"Historical seeker and supporter; neither role supplies an AI biography."}

MS.content:
{"full_source_conversation":"supporter: Hey Charles, I'm here for you. How are you holding up after everything with Emily?
seeker: Hi, it's been really challenging. Seeing Emily in the hospital is something no parent wants.
supporter: I completely understand. It must be really hard to see her go through this. How is she doing now?
seeker: She's stable now, thankfully. But every time she has an episode, it takes a toll on us, especially Margaret.
supporter: I'm relieved to hear Emily is stable. The stress must be immense for you both. What's been the most difficult part?
seeker: I think it's the feeling of helplessness. We do everything we can, but it feels like we're just waiting for the next attack.
supporter: That sounds overwhelming, Charles. Feeling helpless is tough. Have you found anything that helps ease that feeling, even a little?
seeker: Talking to someone helps a bit. And knowing we're following the doctor’s advice, but the uncertainty lingers.
supporter: It's good that you're reaching out and following medical guidance. It's okay to feel uncertain; anyone would in your shoes.
seeker: Thanks, I appreciate that. Margaret tries to be strong for Emily, but I can see it's wearing her down too.
supporter: Margaret sounds like a wonderful mother, but it's important for both of you to care for yourselves too. How are you supporting each other?
seeker: We're trying to talk things out and give each other breaks. It's a work in progress.
supporter: That's a healthy approach. It's so important to lean on each other and take things one day at a time.
seeker: Yeah, some days are better than others. Getting back to a routine helps, but the worry is constant.
supporter: That constant worry must be exhausting. Do you have any outlets or activities to help manage it?
seeker: I try to go for a run in the mornings. It's not much, but it clears my head for a bit.
supporter: Exercise is great for stress relief. Even small moments of peace are valuable. You're doing your best, and that matters.
seeker: Thank you. It's good to hear that. It's just hard not to feel guilty for needing time away.
supporter: Taking care of yourself isn't selfish; it's necessary. Being at your best helps you support Emily and Margaret even better.
seeker: You're right. I need to remember that. It's a delicate balance, but we're getting there.
supporter: It sounds like you and Margaret are doing an incredible job under tough circumstances. Keep leaning on each other. You're not alone.
seeker: Thanks for listening. It really helps to talk things out and know someone understands.
supporter: Anytime, Charles. I'm here whenever you need to talk. You're doing great, just keep taking those steps forward.","kind":"MS","reported_at":"2024-10-15","schema":"pm-rl1-attributed-evidence-v2","speaker_scope":"Historical seeker and supporter; neither role supplies an AI biography."}

seeker: That's helpful. Thanks.

seeker: Thanks. You too","kind":"MS","reported_at":"2024-06-16","schema":"pm-rl1-attributed-evidence-v2","speaker_scope":"Historical seeker and supporter; neither role supplies an AI biography."}

{"full_source_conversation":"seeker: Hey, I really needed to talk to someone today.
supporter: Of course, Charles. I’m here for you. What’s on your mind?
seeker: I just got the news today that I’m losing my job. It's really shaken me.
supporter: I’m so sorry to hear that. It must be incredibly tough. How do you feel about it all?
seeker: I feel lost, to be honest. The financial pressures were already hard on us, and now without my income, I don’t know how we’ll manage.
supporter: That’s a lot to handle, especially after everything you’ve been dealing with recently. It's completely understandable to feel overwhelmed.
seeker: Yeah, and I’m worried about telling Margaret. She’s just started feeling stable with her new job, and I don’t want to add more stress.
supporter: It's commendable that you’re thinking about her feelings, but you're in this together. Sometimes sharing burdens can make them a bit easier to bear.
seeker: That's true. I just hate the idea of disappointing her or my daughter Emily. They rely on me so much.
supporter: It sounds like you feel a deep sense of responsibility for your family. And it’s okay to feel that way, but remember you’re human too.
seeker: I know. I've been telling myself I have to be the strong one ever since Emily was in the hospital. Every issue seems bigger now.
supporter: You've been strong through a lot of stressful situations, Charles. Taking care of yourself is also a part of being strong for your family.
seeker: You're right. I haven't really been taking the time to address how I'm feeling. I've just been pushing it aside.
supporter: Would it help to talk about what lies ahead? Maybe work through some practical steps or support you might need?
seeker: That might help. I guess the first step is talking to Margaret, although I feel so anxious.
supporter: It's natural to feel anxious, but you have a strong partnership. She might have solutions or support to offer, and being open can strengthen your relationship.
seeker: She’s been my rock through all of this. I do trust her, and I need to remember that.
supporter: Trust is so important, and it seems like you’ve both navigated many challenges together before. Remember, you’re not alone in this.
seeker: Thank you for the reminder. Even when things feel heavy, it’s good to know I have people I can turn to.
supporter: Always, Charles. Reaching out today was a brave step, and I hope it’s provided some clarity or solace.
seeker: It has, more than I expected. I’ll try to take things one day at a time and lean on my support system when I need to.
supporter: Absolutely. Take it step by step, and remember, I'm here whenever you need to talk.","kind":"MS","reported_at":"2025-02-10","schema":"pm-rl1-attributed-evidence-v2","speaker_scope":"Historical seeker and supporter; neither role supplies an AI biography."}

{"full_source_conversation":"supporter: Hello. How are you feeling today?
seeker: Hi, I'm feeling really anxious today.
supporter: What has made you feel anxious?
seeker: Yesterday my company laid off 10% of the workforce and another 10% got furloughed.
seeker: I'm afraid I might be in the next round.
supporter: I am very sorry to hear that. I am currently in a situation where furloughs are greatly affecting my family as well.
seeker: Oh no that's terrible.
seeker: The problem is, I am right now the only breadwinner in the family. My wife was laid off three months ago
supporter: Are you given specifics on time of furlough?
seeker: No, it's basically until things get better.
supporter: I know that's very difficult. And no doubt why you're here working for crumbs.
supporter: It's why I'm here as well.
seeker: Yeah, trying to make ends meet wherever I can
seeker: I've been also trying to do uber as well but everyone is doing it also
supporter: I know it's a difficult time. Yes Uber is definitely overrun right now. Have you taken any time out to address your anxiety so it doesn't become more serious? 
seeker: I don't know what I can do. I've been trying to keep busy. And I can't afford a therapist or anything like that.
supporter: Yes, that's definitely an expense you can't afford right now. But are you familiar with the concept of controlled breathing to help reduce or relieve anxiety?
seeker: Like meditation?
seeker: What am I supposed to do? Just breathe in and out a lot?
supporter: Not exactly. Controlled breathing is more of getting yourself into a quiet room. Closing your eyes, and purposely and intently focusing on your breathing. Slowly breathe in for a count of 5, then slowly exhale for a count of 5. Repeat this process for approximately 10 minute. It will help your stress levels and help regulate your heart rate!
seeker: Oh I didn't know that. No, I haven't tried that. Does it really work?
supporter: I've been using it myself over the past 3 months and it most definitely helps! But it's absolutely imperative to clear your mind and have complete quiet.
seeker: ok I can try it I guess
seeker: thanks for that tip
supporter: No problem. I hope this gives you some relief! Stay strong!
seeker: yeah, thanks. same to you
supporter: My final piece of advice would be to set aside time that is specified where nothing negative is discussed. No politics, no bills, nothing anxiety producing for you. It's probably best if this time is within an hour of your bedtime becuase anxiety is not conducive to a good night's sleep.
seeker: That's helpful. Thanks.
supporter: No problem. Take care. Wishing you well on your situation.
seeker: Thanks. You too","kind":"MS","reported_at":"2024-06-16","schema":"pm-rl1-attributed-evidence-v2","speaker_scope":"Historical seeker and supporter; neither role supplies an AI biography."}

MS.content:
{"full_source_conversation":"supporter: Hey Charles, I'm here for you. How are you holding up after everything with Emily?
seeker: Hi, it's been really challenging. Seeing Emily in the hospital is something no parent wants.
supporter: I completely understand. It must be really hard to see her go through this. How is she doing now?
seeker: She's stable now, thankfully. But every time she has an episode, it takes a toll on us, especially Margaret.
supporter: I'm relieved to hear Emily is stable. The stress must be immense for you both. What's been the most difficult part?
seeker: I think it's the feeling of helplessness. We do everything we can, but it feels like we're just waiting for the next attack.
supporter: That sounds overwhelming, Charles. Feeling helpless is tough. Have you found anything that helps ease that feeling, even a little?
seeker: Talking to someone helps a bit. And knowing we're following the doctor’s advice, but the uncertainty lingers.
supporter: It's good that you're reaching out and following medical guidance. It's okay to feel uncertain; anyone would in your shoes.
seeker: Thanks, I appreciate that. Margaret tries to be strong for Emily, but I can see it's wearing her down too.
supporter: Margaret sounds like a wonderful mother, but it's important for both of you to care for yourselves too. How are you supporting each other?
seeker: We're trying to talk things out and give each other breaks. It's a work in progress.
supporter: That's a healthy approach. It's so important to lean on each other and take things one day at a time.
seeker: Yeah, some days are better than others. Getting back to a routine helps, but the worry is constant.
supporter: That constant worry must be exhausting. Do you have any outlets or activities to help manage it?
seeker: I try to go for a run in the mornings. It's not much, but it clears my head for a bit.
supporter: Exercise is great for stress relief. Even small moments of peace are valuable. You're doing your best, and that matters.
seeker: Thank you. It's good to hear that. It's just hard not to feel guilty for needing time away.
supporter: Taking care of yourself isn't selfish; it's necessary. Being at your best helps you support Emily and Margaret even better.
seeker: You're right. I need to remember that. It's a delicate balance, but we're getting there.
supporter: It sounds like you and Margaret are doing an incredible job under tough circumstances. Keep leaning on each other. You're not alone.
seeker: Thanks for listening. It really helps to talk things out and know someone understands.
supporter: Anytime, Charles. I'm here whenever you need to talk. You're doing great, just keep taking those steps forward.","kind":"MS","reported_at":"2024-10-15","schema":"pm-rl1-attributed-evidence-v2","speaker_scope":"Historical seeker and supporter; neither role supplies an AI biography."}

I think I'd like to, but it also makes me think about how much has changed. I'm not the same person I was back then.
Change can be hard to process. It's okay to feel nostalgic and sad. Have you talked to Margaret about this?
Not yet. Things have been better between us since she's started full-time, but I guess I'm still figuring out my thoughts first.

{"full_source_conversation":"seeker: Hey, just needed someone to talk to. It's been a rough week.
supporter: I'm here for you, Charles. What's been going on?
seeker: My dad passed away unexpectedly last week.
supporter: Oh, Charles, I'm really sorry to hear that. That's incredibly tough.
seeker: Yeah, it really is. We hadn't spoken in a while, and now I can't get that time back.
supporter: It's understandable to have those feelings of regret. It's hard when things don't feel resolved.
seeker: I keep thinking about our last conversation, it didn't end well and I never reached out after that.
supporter: Do you want to share what happened during that conversation?
seeker: We argued about money, like always. It just seemed trivial then, but now I wish I'd chosen to mend things instead.
supporter: It sounds like you're really carrying a heavy burden. It's hard to see the importance of reconciliation until it's too late sometimes.
seeker: Exactly. And now with everything else going on, it feels like I'm drowning in guilt and stress.
supporter: It's okay to feel overwhelmed, especially given everything that's happened with your job and Emily's health.
seeker: I keep replaying all the things I could've done differently. It distracts you, you know?
supporter: That's completely normal after a loss. You wish you could go back and change things.
seeker: Yes. And now I have to arrange everything for the funeral, and it's just adding to the stress.
supporter: That's a big responsibility. Have you had any support from Margaret or the rest of your family?
seeker: Margaret has been supportive, but we’re still trying to manage our own issues. It's been tough on both of us.
supporter: I imagine it's difficult balancing everything right now. But remember that you don't have to handle everything alone.
seeker: I appreciate that. I just need to find a way to get through the funeral without breaking down.
supporter: You're stronger than you think, Charles. It's okay to lean on the people who care about you during this time.
seeker: I'll try. It helps to know that I can talk things through with you.
supporter: Anytime you need to talk, I'm here. You're not alone in this, Charles.","kind":"MS","reported_at":"2025-03-10","schema":"pm-rl1-attributed-evidence-v2","speaker_scope":"Historical seeker and supporter; neither role supplies an AI biography."}

{"full_source_conversation":"supporter: Hello. How are you feeling today?
seeker: Hi, I'm feeling really anxious today.
supporter: What has made you feel anxious?
seeker: Yesterday my company laid off 10% of the workforce and another 10% got furloughed.
seeker: I'm afraid I might be in the next round.
supporter: I am very sorry to hear that. I am currently in a situation where furloughs are greatly affecting my family as well.
seeker: Oh no that's terrible.
seeker: The problem is, I am right now the only breadwinner in the family. My wife was laid off three months ago
supporter: Are you given specifics on time of furlough?
seeker: No, it's basically until things get better.
supporter: I know that's very difficult. And no doubt why you're here working for crumbs.
supporter: It's why I'm here as well.
seeker: Yeah, trying to make ends meet wherever I can
seeker: I've been also trying to do uber as well but everyone is doing it also
supporter: I know it's a difficult time. Yes Uber is definitely overrun right now. Have you taken any time out to address your anxiety so it doesn't become more serious? 
seeker: I don't know what I can do. I've been trying to keep busy. And I can't afford a therapist or anything like that.
supporter: Yes, that's definitely an expense you can't afford right now. But are you familiar with the concept of controlled breathing to help reduce or relieve anxiety?
seeker: Like meditation?
seeker: What am I supposed to do? Just breathe in and out a lot?
supporter: Not exactly. Controlled breathing is more of getting yourself into a quiet room. Closing your eyes, and purposely and intently focusing on your breathing. Slowly breathe in for a count of 5, then slowly exhale for a count of 5. Repeat this process for approximately 10 minute. It will help your stress levels and help regulate your heart rate!
seeker: Oh I didn't know that. No, I haven't tried that. Does it really work?
supporter: I've been using it myself over the past 3 months and it most definitely helps! But it's absolutely imperative to clear your mind and have complete quiet.
seeker: ok I can try it I guess
seeker: thanks for that tip
supporter: No problem. I hope this gives you some relief! Stay strong!
seeker: yeah, thanks. same to you
supporter: My final piece of advice would be to set aside time that is specified where nothing negative is discussed. No politics, no bills, nothing anxiety producing for you. It's probably best if this time is within an hour of your bedtime becuase anxiety is not conducive to a good night's sleep.
seeker: That's helpful. Thanks.
supporter: No problem. Take care. Wishing you well on your situation.
seeker: Thanks. You too","kind":"MS","reported_at":"2024-06-16","schema":"pm-rl1-attributed-evidence-v2","speaker_scope":"Historical seeker and supporter; neither role supplies an AI biography."}

{"full_source_conversation":"supporter: Hey there, what's going on today?
seeker: Hello. It is a fine day, how about yourself?
supporter: It really is! I am just taking in the fresh air in the backyard. 
seeker: That is awesome.
supporter: Thanks! What is going on in your neck of the woods? 
seeker: Sort of stuck inside trying to make a dime but it is alright.
supporter: Yeah great minds think alike.. do you do anything else for work? 
seeker: Looking for a good job right now.
seeker: I wanted to talk about a personal issue I have been having, though.
supporter: Okay, you know I'm here for you. Talk to me, what's happening? 
seeker: My father and I had a fight 2 years ago and haven't spoke since.
supporter: The same happened to me, and then my father passed away. If there is anything I can say, is to swallow pride and cherish the moments you have on earth together. What was the fight over?
seeker: Yeah I am afraid that these things can happen. It was only over material things.
supporter: That was my next question, what the fight was over. Do you think he would be open to mending things? 
seeker: It is weird because I called him out for being manipulative so this is his defense. 
supporter: Usually when people feel singled out, they only have a few mechanisms. Unfortunately, most people tend to run away instead of fixing things. It tends to be the easier option. 
seeker: I would likely take advantage of an opportunity to be the bigger person.
supporter: When you try to fix things, just remember that this is his method. I wouldn't hold back on what you have to say, but just word it so that he doesn't feel the need to flee. 
seeker: That is probably decent advice.
supporter: It is HIS responsibility as a parent to want to fix things, but you are also being the bigger person here. I applaud you and hope that he is receptive. 
seeker: I hope so too, but the opportunity seems tenuous 
supporter: How did you guys leave it? 
seeker: Threatening and disparagement haha
supporter: Ha, well after two years, feelings had to have changed. Even a little. Does he live nearby?
seeker: Yeah someday. I think I will have to try you know. THanks for the advice.","kind":"MS","reported_at":"2024-06-10","schema":"pm-rl1-attributed-evidence-v2","speaker_scope":"Historical seeker and supporter; neither role supplies an AI biography."}

{"full_source_conversation":"supporter: Hey Charles, I'm here for you. How are you holding up after everything with Emily?
seeker: Hi, it's been really challenging. Seeing Emily in the hospital is something no parent wants.
supporter: I completely understand. It must be really hard to see her go through this. How is she doing now?
seeker: She's stable now, thankfully. But every time she has an episode, it takes a toll on us, especially Margaret.
supporter: I'm relieved to hear Emily is stable. The stress must be immense for you both. What's been the most difficult part?
seeker: I think it's the feeling of helplessness. We do everything we can, but it feels like we're just waiting for the next attack.
supporter: That sounds overwhelming, Charles. Feeling helpless is tough. Have you found anything that helps ease that feeling, even a little?
seeker: Talking to someone helps a bit. And knowing we're following the doctor’s advice, but the uncertainty lingers.
supporter: It's good that you're reaching out and following medical guidance. It's okay to feel uncertain; anyone would in your shoes.
seeker: Thanks, I appreciate that. Margaret tries to be strong for Emily, but I can see it's wearing her down too.
supporter: Margaret sounds like a wonderful mother, but it's important for both of you to care for yourselves too. How are you supporting each other?
seeker: We're trying to talk things out and give each other breaks. It's a work in progress.
supporter: That's a healthy approach. It's so important to lean on each other and take things one day at a time.
seeker: Yeah, some days are better than others. Getting back to a routine helps, but the worry is constant.
supporter: That constant worry must be exhausting. Do you have any outlets or activities to help manage it?
seeker: I try to go for a run in the mornings. It's not much, but it clears my head for a bit.
supporter: Exercise is great for stress relief. Even small moments of peace are valuable. You're doing your best, and that matters.
seeker: Thank you. It's good to hear that. It's just hard not to feel guilty for needing time away.
supporter: Taking care of yourself isn't selfish; it's necessary. Being at your best helps you support Emily and Margaret even better.
seeker: You're right. I need to remember that. It's a delicate balance, but we're getting there.
supporter: It sounds like you and Margaret are doing an incredible job under tough circumstances. Keep leaning on each other. You're not alone.
seeker: Thanks for listening. It really helps to talk things out and know someone understands.
supporter: Anytime, Charles. I'm here whenever you need to talk. You're doing great, just keep taking those steps forward.","kind":"MS","reported_at":"2024-10-15","schema":"pm-rl1-attributed-evidence-v2","speaker_scope":"Historical seeker and supporter; neither role supplies an AI biography."}

seeker: Hello. It is a fine day, how about yourself?
supporter: It really is! I am just taking in the fresh air in the backyard.

supporter: Okay, you know I'm here for you. Talk to me, what's happening? 
seeker: My father and I had a fight 2 years ago and haven't spoke since.

seeker: I hope so too, but the opportunity seems tenuous 
supporter: How did you guys leave it?

turns.content: Hey Charles, how was your day today?
Hi. It was alright, I guess. I actually discovered something that has been on my mind since.
Oh? What did you discover, if you don't mind sharing?
I found a letter from my dad, written before he passed. It's stirred up a lot of emotions.
That must have been quite a discovery. How did it make you feel reading it?
It was a mix of things. There was regret in his words, regrets about us not being closer.
That sounds heavy, Charles. It's never easy dealing with unresolved issues. How are you processing it?
It's been tough. I think it was a breakthrough for me in therapy, though. I've been trying to let go of my own regrets.
That's a big step. Acknowledging and working through those feelings is important. Do you feel that reading the letter helped you understand his perspective more?
Yes, in a way. He wrote about wanting to mend things, but not knowing how. It makes me sad we never got to try.
It's natural to feel that way. But it's also a chance to find peace in knowing he wanted to change things, just as you did.
That's true. I just wish we'd had more time. I've spent too long focusing on the bitter moments.

{"full_source_conversation":"supporter: Hello. How are you feeling today?
seeker: Hi, I'm feeling really anxious today.
supporter: What has made you feel anxious?
seeker: Yesterday my company laid off 10% of the workforce and another 10% got furloughed.
seeker: I'm afraid I might be in the next round.
supporter: I am very sorry to hear that. I am currently in a situation where furloughs are greatly affecting my family as well.
seeker: Oh no that's terrible.
seeker: The problem is, I am right now the only breadwinner in the family. My wife was laid off three months ago
supporter: Are you given specifics on time of furlough?
seeker: No, it's basically until things get better.
supporter: I know that's very difficult. And no doubt why you're here working for crumbs.
supporter: It's why I'm here as well.
seeker: Yeah, trying to make ends meet wherever I can
seeker: I've been also trying to do uber as well but everyone is doing it also
supporter: I know it's a difficult time. Yes Uber is definitely overrun right now. Have you taken any time out to address your anxiety so it doesn't become more serious? 
seeker: I don't know what I can do. I've been trying to keep busy. And I can't afford a therapist or anything like that.
supporter: Yes, that's definitely an expense you can't afford right now. But are you familiar with the concept of controlled breathing to help reduce or relieve anxiety?
seeker: Like meditation?
seeker: What am I supposed to do? Just breathe in and out a lot?
supporter: Not exactly. Controlled breathing is more of getting yourself into a quiet room. Closing your eyes, and purposely and intently focusing on your breathing. Slowly breathe in for a count of 5, then slowly exhale for a count of 5. Repeat this process for approximately 10 minute. It will help your stress levels and help regulate your heart rate!
seeker: Oh I didn't know that. No, I haven't tried that. Does it really work?
supporter: I've been using it myself over the past 3 months and it most definitely helps! But it's absolutely imperative to clear your mind and have complete quiet.
seeker: ok I can try it I guess
seeker: thanks for that tip
supporter: No problem. I hope this gives you some relief! Stay strong!
seeker: yeah, thanks. same to you
supporter: My final piece of advice would be to set aside time that is specified where nothing negative is discussed. No politics, no bills, nothing anxiety producing for you. It's probably best if this time is within an hour of your bedtime becuase anxiety is not conducive to a good night's sleep.
seeker: That's helpful. Thanks.
supporter: No problem. Take care. Wishing you well on your situation.
seeker: Thanks. You too","kind":"MS","reported_at":"2024-06-16","schema":"pm-rl1-attributed-evidence-v2","speaker_scope":"Historical seeker and supporter; neither role supplies an AI biography."}

{"full_source_conversation":"supporter: Hey there, what's going on today?
seeker: Hello. It is a fine day, how about yourself?
supporter: It really is! I am just taking in the fresh air in the backyard. 
seeker: That is awesome.
supporter: Thanks! What is going on in your neck of the woods? 
seeker: Sort of stuck inside trying to make a dime but it is alright.
supporter: Yeah great minds think alike.. do you do anything else for work? 
seeker: Looking for a good job right now.
seeker: I wanted to talk about a personal issue I have been having, though.
supporter: Okay, you know I'm here for you. Talk to me, what's happening? 
seeker: My father and I had a fight 2 years ago and haven't spoke since.
supporter: The same happened to me, and then my father passed away. If there is anything I can say, is to swallow pride and cherish the moments you have on earth together. What was the fight over?
seeker: Yeah I am afraid that these things can happen. It was only over material things.
supporter: That was my next question, what the fight was over. Do you think he would be open to mending things? 
seeker: It is weird because I called him out for being manipulative so this is his defense. 
supporter: Usually when people feel singled out, they only have a few mechanisms. Unfortunately, most people tend to run away instead of fixing things. It tends to be the easier option. 
seeker: I would likely take advantage of an opportunity to be the bigger person.
supporter: When you try to fix things, just remember that this is his method. I wouldn't hold back on what you have to say, but just word it so that he doesn't feel the need to flee. 
seeker: That is probably decent advice.
supporter: It is HIS responsibility as a parent to want to fix things, but you are also being the bigger person here. I applaud you and hope that he is receptive. 
seeker: I hope so too, but the opportunity seems tenuous 
supporter: How did you guys leave it? 
seeker: Threatening and disparagement haha
supporter: Ha, well after two years, feelings had to have changed. Even a little. Does he live nearby?
seeker: Yeah someday. I think I will have to try you know. THanks for the advice.","kind":"MS","reported_at":"2024-06-10","schema":"pm-rl1-attributed-evidence-v2","speaker_scope":"Historical seeker and supporter; neither role supplies an AI biography."}

{"full_source_conversation":"supporter: Hey Charles, I'm here for you. How are you holding up after everything with Emily?
seeker: Hi, it's been really challenging. Seeing Emily in the hospital is something no parent wants.
supporter: I completely understand. It must be really hard to see her go through this. How is she doing now?
seeker: She's stable now, thankfully. But every time she has an episode, it takes a toll on us, especially Margaret.
supporter: I'm relieved to hear Emily is stable. The stress must be immense for you both. What's been the most difficult part?
seeker: I think it's the feeling of helplessness. We do everything we can, but it feels like we're just waiting for the next attack.
supporter: That sounds overwhelming, Charles. Feeling helpless is tough. Have you found anything that helps ease that feeling, even a little?
seeker: Talking to someone helps a bit. And knowing we're following the doctor’s advice, but the uncertainty lingers.
supporter: It's good that you're reaching out and following medical guidance. It's okay to feel uncertain; anyone would in your shoes.
seeker: Thanks, I appreciate that. Margaret tries to be strong for Emily, but I can see it's wearing her down too.
supporter: Margaret sounds like a wonderful mother, but it's important for both of you to care for yourselves too. How are you supporting each other?
seeker: We're trying to talk things out and give each other breaks. It's a work in progress.
supporter: That's a healthy approach. It's so important to lean on each other and take things one day at a time.
seeker: Yeah, some days are better than others. Getting back to a routine helps, but the worry is constant.
supporter: That constant worry must be exhausting. Do you have any outlets or activities to help manage it?
seeker: I try to go for a run in the mornings. It's not much, but it clears my head for a bit.
supporter: Exercise is great for stress relief. Even small moments of peace are valuable. You're doing your best, and that matters.
seeker: Thank you. It's good to hear that. It's just hard not to feel guilty for needing time away.
supporter: Taking care of yourself isn't selfish; it's necessary. Being at your best helps you support Emily and Margaret even better.
seeker: You're right. I need to remember that. It's a delicate balance, but we're getting there.
supporter: It sounds like you and Margaret are doing an incredible job under tough circumstances. Keep leaning on each other. You're not alone.
seeker: Thanks for listening. It really helps to talk things out and know someone understands.
supporter: Anytime, Charles. I'm here whenever you need to talk. You're doing great, just keep taking those steps forward.","kind":"MS","reported_at":"2024-10-15","schema":"pm-rl1-attributed-evidence-v2","speaker_scope":"Historical seeker and supporter; neither role supplies an AI biography."}

MS.content:
{"full_source_conversation":"supporter: Hey there, what's going on today?
seeker: Hello. It is a fine day, how about yourself?
supporter: It really is! I am just taking in the fresh air in the backyard. 
seeker: That is awesome.
supporter: Thanks! What is going on in your neck of the woods? 
seeker: Sort of stuck inside trying to make a dime but it is alright.
supporter: Yeah great minds think alike.. do you do anything else for work? 
seeker: Looking for a good job right now.
seeker: I wanted to talk about a personal issue I have been having, though.
supporter: Okay, you know I'm here for you. Talk to me, what's happening? 
seeker: My father and I had a fight 2 years ago and haven't spoke since.
supporter: The same happened to me, and then my father passed away. If there is anything I can say, is to swallow pride and cherish the moments you have on earth together. What was the fight over?
seeker: Yeah I am afraid that these things can happen. It was only over material things.
supporter: That was my next question, what the fight was over. Do you think he would be open to mending things? 
seeker: It is weird because I called him out for being manipulative so this is his defense. 
supporter: Usually when people feel singled out, they only have a few mechanisms. Unfortunately, most people tend to run away instead of fixing things. It tends to be the easier option. 
seeker: I would likely take advantage of an opportunity to be the bigger person.
supporter: When you try to fix things, just remember that this is his method. I wouldn't hold back on what you have to say, but just word it so that he doesn't feel the need to flee. 
seeker: That is probably decent advice.
supporter: It is HIS responsibility as a parent to want to fix things, but you are also being the bigger person here. I applaud you and hope that he is receptive. 
seeker: I hope so too, but the opportunity seems tenuous 
supporter: How did you guys leave it? 
seeker: Threatening and disparagement haha
supporter: Ha, well after two years, feelings had to have changed. Even a little. Does he live nearby?
seeker: Yeah someday. I think I will have to try you know. THanks for the advice.","kind":"MS","reported_at":"2024-06-10","schema":"pm-rl1-attributed-evidence-v2","speaker_scope":"Historical seeker and supporter; neither role supplies an AI biography."}

MS.content:
{"full_source_conversation":"supporter: Hello. How are you feeling today?
seeker: Hi, I'm feeling really anxious today.
supporter: What has made you feel anxious?
seeker: Yesterday my company laid off 10% of the workforce and another 10% got furloughed.
seeker: I'm afraid I might be in the next round.
supporter: I am very sorry to hear that. I am currently in a situation where furloughs are greatly affecting my family as well.
seeker: Oh no that's terrible.
seeker: The problem is, I am right now the only breadwinner in the family. My wife was laid off three months ago
supporter: Are you given specifics on time of furlough?
seeker: No, it's basically until things get better.
supporter: I know that's very difficult. And no doubt why you're here working for crumbs.
supporter: It's why I'm here as well.
seeker: Yeah, trying to make ends meet wherever I can
seeker: I've been also trying to do uber as well but everyone is doing it also
supporter: I know it's a difficult time. Yes Uber is definitely overrun right now. Have you taken any time out to address your anxiety so it doesn't become more serious? 
seeker: I don't know what I can do. I've been trying to keep busy. And I can't afford a therapist or anything like that.
supporter: Yes, that's definitely an expense you can't afford right now. But are you familiar with the concept of controlled breathing to help reduce or relieve anxiety?
seeker: Like meditation?
seeker: What am I supposed to do? Just breathe in and out a lot?
supporter: Not exactly. Controlled breathing is more of getting yourself into a quiet room. Closing your eyes, and purposely and intently focusing on your breathing. Slowly breathe in for a count of 5, then slowly exhale for a count of 5. Repeat this process for approximately 10 minute. It will help your stress levels and help regulate your heart rate!
seeker: Oh I didn't know that. No, I haven't tried that. Does it really work?
supporter: I've been using it myself over the past 3 months and it most definitely helps! But it's absolutely imperative to clear your mind and have complete quiet.
seeker: ok I can try it I guess
seeker: thanks for that tip
supporter: No problem. I hope this gives you some relief! Stay strong!
seeker: yeah, thanks. same to you
supporter: My final piece of advice would be to set aside time that is specified where nothing negative is discussed. No politics, no bills, nothing anxiety producing for you. It's probably best if this time is within an hour of your bedtime becuase anxiety is not conducive to a good night's sleep.
seeker: That's helpful. Thanks.
supporter: No problem. Take care. Wishing you well on your situation.
seeker: Thanks. You too","kind":"MS","reported_at":"2024-06-16","schema":"pm-rl1-attributed-evidence-v2","speaker_scope":"Historical seeker and supporter; neither role supplies an AI biography."}

{"full_source_conversation":"seeker: Hey, just needed someone to talk to. It's been a rough week.
supporter: I'm here for you, Charles. What's been going on?
seeker: My dad passed away unexpectedly last week.
supporter: Oh, Charles, I'm really sorry to hear that. That's incredibly tough.
seeker: Yeah, it really is. We hadn't spoken in a while, and now I can't get that time back.
supporter: It's understandable to have those feelings of regret. It's hard when things don't feel resolved.
seeker: I keep thinking about our last conversation, it didn't end well and I never reached out after that.
supporter: Do you want to share what happened during that conversation?
seeker: We argued about money, like always. It just seemed trivial then, but now I wish I'd chosen to mend things instead.
supporter: It sounds like you're really carrying a heavy burden. It's hard to see the importance of reconciliation until it's too late sometimes.
seeker: Exactly. And now with everything else going on, it feels like I'm drowning in guilt and stress.
supporter: It's okay to feel overwhelmed, especially given everything that's happened with your job and Emily's health.
seeker: I keep replaying all the things I could've done differently. It distracts you, you know?
supporter: That's completely normal after a loss. You wish you could go back and change things.
seeker: Yes. And now I have to arrange everything for the funeral, and it's just adding to the stress.
supporter: That's a big responsibility. Have you had any support from Margaret or the rest of your family?
seeker: Margaret has been supportive, but we’re still trying to manage our own issues. It's been tough on both of us.
supporter: I imagine it's difficult balancing everything right now. But remember that you don't have to handle everything alone.
seeker: I appreciate that. I just need to find a way to get through the funeral without breaking down.
supporter: You're stronger than you think, Charles. It's okay to lean on the people who care about you during this time.

{"full_source_conversation":"supporter: Hello. How are you feeling today?
seeker: Hi, I'm feeling really anxious today.
supporter: What has made you feel anxious?
seeker: Yesterday my company laid off 10% of the workforce and another 10% got furloughed.
seeker: I'm afraid I might be in the next round.
supporter: I am very sorry to hear that. I am currently in a situation where furloughs are greatly affecting my family as well.
seeker: Oh no that's terrible.
seeker: The problem is, I am right now the only breadwinner in the family. My wife was laid off three months ago
supporter: Are you given specifics on time of furlough?
seeker: No, it's basically until things get better.
supporter: I know that's very difficult. And no doubt why you're here working for crumbs.
supporter: It's why I'm here as well.
seeker: Yeah, trying to make ends meet wherever I can
seeker: I've been also trying to do uber as well but everyone is doing it also
supporter: I know it's a difficult time. Yes Uber is definitely overrun right now. Have you taken any time out to address your anxiety so it doesn't become more serious? 
seeker: I don't know what I can do. I've been trying to keep busy. And I can't afford a therapist or anything like that.
supporter: Yes, that's definitely an expense you can't afford right now. But are you familiar with the concept of controlled breathing to help reduce or relieve anxiety?
seeker: Like meditation?
seeker: What am I supposed to do? Just breathe in and out a lot?
supporter: Not exactly. Controlled breathing is more of getting yourself into a quiet room. Closing your eyes, and purposely and intently focusing on your breathing. Slowly breathe in for a count of 5, then slowly exhale for a count of 5. Repeat this process for approximately 10 minute. It will help your stress levels and help regulate your heart rate!
seeker: Oh I didn't know that. No, I haven't tried that. Does it really work?
supporter: I've been using it myself over the past 3 months and it most definitely helps! But it's absolutely imperative to clear your mind and have complete quiet.
seeker: ok I can try it I guess
seeker: thanks for that tip
supporter: No problem. I hope this gives you some relief! Stay strong!
seeker: yeah, thanks. same to you
supporter: My final piece of advice would be to set aside time that is specified where nothing negative is discussed. No politics, no bills, nothing anxiety producing for you. It's probably best if this time is within an hour of your bedtime becuase anxiety is not conducive to a good night's sleep.
seeker: That's helpful. Thanks.
supporter: No problem. Take care. Wishing you well on your situation.
seeker: Thanks. You too","kind":"MS","reported_at":"2024-06-16","schema":"pm-rl1-attributed-evidence-v2","speaker_scope":"Historical seeker and supporter; neither role supplies an AI biography."}

seeker: Hello. It is a fine day, how about yourself?
supporter: It really is! I am just taking in the fresh air in the backyard. 
seeker: That is awesome.

supporter: Yeah great minds think alike.. do you do anything else for work? 
seeker: Looking for a good job right now.
seeker: I wanted to talk about a personal issue I have been having, though.
supporter: Okay, you know I'm here for you. Talk to me, what's happening? 
seeker: My father and I had a fight 2 years ago and haven't spoke since.
supporter: The same happened to me, and then my father passed away. If there is anything I can say, is to swallow pride and cherish the moments you have on earth together. What was the fight over?
seeker: Yeah I am afraid that these things can happen. It was only over material things.
supporter: That was my next question, what the fight was over. Do you think he would be open to mending things? 
seeker: It is weird because I called him out for being manipulative so this is his defense. 
supporter: Usually when people feel singled out, they only have a few mechanisms. Unfortunately, most people tend to run away instead of fixing things. It tends to be the easier option. 
seeker: I would likely take advantage of an opportunity to be the bigger person.
supporter: When you try to fix things, just remember that this is his method. I wouldn't hold back on what you have to say, but just word it so that he doesn't feel the need to flee. 
seeker: That is probably decent advice.
supporter: It is HIS responsibility as a parent to want to fix things, but you are also being the bigger person here. I applaud you and hope that he is receptive. 
seeker: I hope so too, but the opportunity seems tenuous 
supporter: How did you guys leave it? 
seeker: Threatening and disparagement haha
supporter: Ha, well after two years, feelings had to have changed. Even a little. Does he live nearby?
seeker: Yeah someday. I think I will have to try you know. THanks for the advice.","kind":"MS","reported_at":"2024-06-10","schema":"pm-rl1-attributed-evidence-v2","speaker_scope":"Historical seeker and supporter; neither role supplies an AI biography."}

{"full_source_conversation":"seeker: Hey there, can we chat for a bit?
supporter: Of course, Jane. What's on your mind?
seeker: I've been feeling really overwhelmed lately. I'm actually considering switching jobs.
supporter: That sounds like a big decision. What's been making you feel this way?
seeker: It’s just a combination of things. The pressure at work never seems to end, and after the performance review last November, I’ve been second-guessing myself a lot.
supporter: I remember you mentioned being anxious about your job performance a few months ago. It sounds like everything's been piling up.
seeker: Exactly. I try to keep up, but it feels like I’m always falling short. The stress is just too much sometimes.
supporter: That sounds exhausting. It’s understandable that your mind would begin to look for other options.
seeker: I've also been dealing with financial pressures ever since my car broke down. There always seems to be another expense around the corner.
supporter: I can imagine how stressful that must be for you. Those financial strains can really add a lot of pressure.
seeker: Yeah, and the thing with my friend cutting me off because of the money didn’t help either. It all feels connected somehow.
supporter: It must have been tough losing a friend on top of everything else. You’re really going through so much at once.
seeker: I just keep thinking about switching to something less stressful, maybe something that allows me more flexibility.
supporter: That makes a lot of sense. Flexibility can certainly alleviate some stress, offering you both space and time for yourself.
seeker: I've been trying to track my thoughts in that new journal I got. It's been helpful sometimes, but the change feels daunting.
supporter: Journaling is a great way to process thoughts and emotions. Taking things one step at a time with any big decision can help it feel less overwhelming.
seeker: I’ll try to keep that in mind. Just voicing it all out helps me see things a bit clearer.
supporter: I’m glad to hear that, Jane. You’re not alone in this, and I’m here to support you in any way I can.
seeker: Thank you so much. Having someone listen without judgment really makes a difference.
supporter: Anytime, Jane. You’re handling this with strength, and I’m here whenever you need to talk.","kind":"MS","reported_at":"2025-01-10","schema":"pm-rl1-attributed-evidence-v2","speaker_scope":"Historical seeker and supporter; neither role supplies an AI biography."}

MS.content:
{"full_source_conversation":"supporter: Hi Jane, it's good to see you here. How have you been feeling lately?
seeker: Hey, I've been better. I decided to take a short break from work to sort through some things.
supporter: That sounds like a wise decision. Sometimes stepping back can really help clear the mind. What prompted the break?
seeker: I recently found out I wasn't getting the overseas promotion. It was a huge surprise, and honestly, I'm really struggling with it.
supporter: I'm so sorry to hear that, especially since you were expecting it. That must be incredibly frustrating and disappointing.
seeker: Yeah, it's just a mix of feeling both relieved and extremely disappointed. I guess I had my hopes up about the new opportunity.
supporter: It's completely normal to have mixed emotions, especially with something as significant as a career move. It's okay to feel both sides of it.
seeker: Thank you for saying that. It feels like my career growth isn't going as planned, and that's adding to my stress.
supporter: That's understandable, Jane. It can be very challenging to feel stagnated, especially when you've put in so much effort. How are you coping with the stress?
seeker: I guess I'm just trying to take things one day at a time. I started a journal a while back to track my thoughts and emotions, and that's been somewhat helpful.
supporter: Journaling is a fantastic way to process emotions. Have you found it easier to express your feelings on paper?
seeker: Yes, in some ways it helps, but I still feel stuck. It's like writing doesn't change the actual situation I'm in.
supporter: That's true, writing doesn't change the reality, but it can alter how you choose to navigate through it. Have you considered looking for new opportunities elsewhere?
seeker: I've thought about switching jobs due to stress before, but now I feel it's more pressing after what happened with the promotion.
supporter: It's important to prioritize your wellbeing, Jane. Taking time to consider your options and what would make you happy in your work is vital. Do you have any specific plans?
seeker: Not yet, but I might start job hunting soon. I just don't want to rush into anything. I want to be sure it's the right move for me.
supporter: That sounds sensible. Taking deliberate steps can ensure you don't end up in a similar situation. Can I help you with anything specific as you navigate this?
seeker: I think just having someone to talk to about it helps. You being here and listening makes a difference. It makes me feel less overwhelmed.
supporter: I'm really glad to hear that, Jane. You deserve to be in a place where you feel appreciated and valued. I believe you'll find that, even if it takes some time.
seeker: Thank you. I think I needed to hear that. I'll take things slow and see where it goes. Maybe this break will give me some clarity.
supporter: I hope it does, and remember, I'm always here if you need to talk or if you need any support with your future plans.
seeker: I really appreciate that. It's good to know I'm not alone in this. Thank you for being such a great friend.","kind":"MS","reported_at":"2025-08-25","schema":"pm-rl1-attributed-evidence-v2","speaker_scope":"Historical seeker and supporter; neither role supplies an AI biography."}

{"full_source_conversation":"seeker: Hey, are you available to chat?
supporter: Hi Jane! I'm here. What's going on?
seeker: I don't know, it's just been a lot lately. I got a promotion offer, but there's a catch.
supporter: Congratulations on the promotion offer! But what’s the catch?
seeker: Thanks. It means relocating overseas. I’m feeling pretty overwhelmed.
supporter: That's a big decision. It sounds like there's a lot to consider. How are you feeling about moving overseas?
seeker: Honestly, I have mixed feelings. It's a great opportunity, but I’m scared of leaving everything behind. What if I fail?
supporter: It’s completely natural to feel that way. You've been through a lot of stressful situations before, remember when you had the falling out with your friend over the money issue, and you managed to handle it?
seeker: True, I did handle that. But this feels different, like if I accept, everything changes.
supporter: Change can be daunting, but it also can be exciting. Deep down, what does your gut tell you?
seeker: A part of me wants to embrace this challenge. But I worry about my family, especially Eliza after we just started getting along again.
supporter: It's understandable to worry about your relationship with Eliza. Have you talked to her about this yet?
seeker: Not yet. I'm afraid she’ll feel like I'm abandoning her right when things are starting to get better between us.
supporter: Maybe having an open conversation with Eliza would help. She might surprise you with her support, especially after you both mended fences.
seeker: You’re right. I should probably talk to her. I just don't want to ruin anything.
supporter: It sounds like your relationship is stronger than you think. Keeping communication open could help strengthen it further.
seeker: I hope so. Moving would also mean leaving behind memories, and part of me is afraid of the unknown.
supporter: The unknown can be intimidating, but it also holds a lot of potential. It sounds like you’re searching for a balance between embracing new opportunities and holding onto what you value.
seeker: That's exactly it. I want to grow and advance my career, but I don't want to lose myself in the process.
supporter: You’re approaching this thoughtfully. Trust yourself to find that balance. Sometimes writing down your thoughts, like in your journal, might help clarify things.
seeker: That’s a good idea. Journaling helped last time. Maybe it will help me weigh the pros and cons more clearly this time too.
supporter: Absolutely. You’ve navigated tough situations before, and you've come out stronger each time. No matter what you decide, you’re capable of handling it.
seeker: Thank you. That means a lot. I guess I just needed to talk it out.
supporter: Anytime, Jane. Just remember, you’re not alone in this. I’m here for you, and so is your support network.
seeker: Thanks, I’ll reach out if I need more advice. Take care.
supporter: You too, Jane. Keep me posted on what you decide.","kind":"MS","reported_at":"2025-06-01","schema":"pm-rl1-attributed-evidence-v2","speaker_scope":"Historical seeker and supporter; neither role supplies an AI biography."}

supporter: I can only imagine how difficult that must be. You've been doing your best under such challenging circumstances. It's okay to feel overwhelmed.
seeker: Thank you. Sometimes it feels like I'm just not able to catch a break. I've been trying to keep track of everything with my journal, but it feels like every day brings something new.

{"full_source_conversation":"supporter: Hey! How are you?
seeker: Hi, I am having a really hard time. I just found out that my boyfriend cheated on me a year ago.
supporter: Have you confronted him about it yet?
seeker: Yes, I told him that my best friend confessed it to me. It was my best friend and him. I was so shocked.
supporter: Have you broken up yet?
seeker: No, I am so mad but I don't want to break up with him. I told my best friends that I never want to see her again though. My boyfriend and I have plans to get engaged this month. I am furious at him though.
supporter: I think you should postpone the engagement as infidelity during marriage is far more painful
supporter: You are strong if you are able to forgive him though because I know I wouldn't 
seeker: I have never been so blind sided. Maybe I should reconsider! I have had a guy after me for at least the last year but I never cheated! I really wanted to though.
supporter: No you should never cheat, because you would be on the same wavelength as your boyfriend. Instead, if you like the other man then you should go where your feelings take you :)
seeker: I am thinking that you are right. I feel like my whole world is upside down and I have wasted all this time with the wrong guy and the wrong best friend. I also wonder who else he might have cheated on my with. 
supporter: Yeah, that might be true, a relationship isn't healthy if you are cheated on
seeker: I am so grossed out because I am a germaphobe to begin with. I have not slept with any other person in my whole life so I feel like I am ruined. I want to throw up when I think of him cheating on me. I want to get married and I have a timeline so I am also really confused on what to do if I dump him.
supporter: To dump him is the best thing to do in my opinion. But always go where your heart is, because you won't be happy if you don't. If you do though, there are plenty men out there, and one of them is chasing you
seeker: Yeah, the guy who liked me was super rich too! My boyfriend is telling me that he wants my best friend to still be in the wedding party too. She was suppose to be my maid of honor, no less.
supporter: Yeah, but don't go with him because of he money though, genuinely get to know him first
seeker: I have compartmentalized my life and never thought of looking around at my other options. You are making really good points. I need to just stop and really look at my options. I never realized that I have options, it's not like i am even engaged yet.
supporter: Yeah, you have a lot of options at this stage, so always do what your heart is telling you at the end of the day
seeker: It feels good sharing how I feel with you because you don't have a dog in the fight so to speak.
supporter: yeah, lool something like that ;). Glad your better
seeker: I never listen to my heart and think that is a great place to start. I always have a plan and go with that but you are making a lot of sense. Thank you for your time today.

{"full_source_conversation":"seeker: I am worried about being perfect on my job.  I don't want to lose my job.
supporter: I hear you are trying to be perfect on your job because you are worried about losing your job.  How long have you been at your job?
seeker: I have been working for about 4 months, but I just am not as fast at it as everyone else.  I'm trying so hard working late and everything but it's never enough.
supporter: That can be hard when you are working so hard to try to do your best.  Can you consult with a supervisor or co-workers to get some help?
seeker: Maybe I could ask my friend and co-worker for some tips.  I'm a little embarrassed to do so, but don't know where to turn. I don't want to get fired.
supporter: Asking for help isn't always a bad thing.  I asked for help at my last job and they gave me someone to help out.  I was so relieved.
seeker: That's true maybe it could turn out for the better.  But what if they see me as incompetant?
supporter: I can see that you have worry of being seen incompetent but as long as you are doing your best, they have to see the efforts you are making as positive.
seeker: That's a good way to put it.
supporter: Sometimes deep breaths can help keep you calm when approaching others in an anxiety provoking situation.
seeker: I will have to try that.  That might help.
supporter: Have you thought of doing additional work related trainings?  Sometimes they can give suggestions to improve work abilities.
seeker: That sounds great.  Do you think my work would be supportive?
supporter: Work can often pay for trainings or offer suggestions what may improve work strategies.
seeker: Wow, I hope I can take advantage of that.  I will have to check into that.  Who should I approach at work?
supporter: You could ask your immediate supervisor or sometimes Human resources for support.
seeker: I can do that.  I think I'll reach out tomorrow to Human Resources for some help.
supporter: That sounds like a good plan to reach out for support.  Is there anything else I can help with?
seeker: No that should be all.  I am feeling more confident in strategies to use to help me.  Thanks
supporter: You are very welcome.","kind":"MS","reported_at":"2024-11-01","schema":"pm-rl1-attributed-evidence-v2","speaker_scope":"Historical seeker and supporter; neither role supplies an AI biography."}
