MS.content:
{"full_source_conversation":"seeker: Yo
supporter: Hi, how are you doing?
seeker: I am decent. I am here because my friend talks way too much on the phone, and it frustrates me.
seeker: They never want to hang up, and the talk can literally go on for hours.
supporter: It sounds like it would be quite frustrating for your friend to talk way too much on the phone. 
seeker: No, he loves it! I'm the one who hates it.
supporter: My goodness! How do they respond when you ask to end the conversation?
seeker: I tell him, but he just doesn't get it. Or, he says he understands, but then just goes back to talking!
seeker: Or, he may finally end the talk, but the next time we talk, he will just do it all over again!
supporter: I wonder what it would be like for him if you hung up the phone even after he said he still wanted to talk.
supporter: Wow--that does sound annoying that he will repeat the same pattern the next time.
seeker: He will literally talk up to 10 minutes without letting you have a word in. As far as that advice, I have hung up, but he gets extremely offended easily.
supporter: That sounds really difficult if he gets offended so easily. I find it hard to talk to some of those kinds of friends.
seeker: I'm at my wits end. I tell him all the time. "You talk too much. You gotta stop talking at me. You gotta give the other person a turn. You gotta respect other's time."
supporter: What do you get out of the friendship with this other person?
seeker: Well, I've been friends with him for a long time. He's funny and can have interesting perspectives on things. Also, we have done a lot together in the past.
supporter: That sounds like a lot that the two of you have been through. Were there other times that your friends was more equally responsive or attuned to you in conversations?
seeker: Oh, yes, I have other friends in conversations who can take turns and understand the concept of time just fine.
seeker: I just don't know what to do about this guy in particular. I still want to be his friend, but he just doesn't change.
supporter: I wonder if there is anything nice you could do for yourself when you are talking to him that would make it easier to talk to him.
seeker: Do you think I should just have a timer that goes off at 1 minute and let it beep in his face if he goes on for too long to train him like a monkey?
supporter: I can see that you are feeling upset and angry when he talks so much and that is totally understandable. 
seeker: I just need a method. Talking to him is just not working.
seeker: He is hard to condition.
supporter: Would it hurt his feelings to use a timer like that? It may for some other people. 
seeker: Yea, but I might be able to slip some humour in there to take the edge off because it is so silly.
supporter: Humor is really helpful for a lot of people. 
seeker: Any other ideas?
supporter: Sometimes, people draw or do something else distracting with their hands when talking to someone who dominates the conversation.
seeker: So your option is to start just doing something else when he is talking? He might get the message in a subtle way?
supporter: Sometimes that is a less offensive way to retrain someone who is being obnoxious or dominant and yet who is easily offended. And, it can help preserve your sense of being grounded.
supporter: The strategy works well for me with some of my family members who seem like they will never change. But, with distraction, I enjoy them all the more.
seeker: This is true, and it isn't bade advice. Haha! That is funny. Yes, maybe I should find something to carry around with me that I can enjoy.
seeker: I don't really like to draw...
supporter: Is there anything else that you like to do that would be distracting while also letting you somewhat participate in the conversation?
seeker: Yes, perhaps I should just use the internet when he starts talking too much. 
seeker: I have a phone.
supporter: That sounds really helpful. Sometimes people also play phone games or with a fidget spinner. I like your idea of looking on the internet.
seeker: This solves the problem in person, but it doesn't solve the talks over the phone, but it has been 15 minutes now and this has been helpful enough. Thank you for your solutions. You have been very supportive and kind to me
seeker: I don't want to take up any more of your time. It has been a good conversation. 
supporter: You are very welcome. I wish you all the best!
seeker: Goodbye. You as well.
supporter: Bye!","kind":"MS","reported_at":"2024-07-15","schema":"pm-rl1-attributed-evidence-v2","speaker_scope":"Historical seeker and supporter; neither role supplies an AI biography."}

{"full_source_conversation":"supporter: Hi there, how are you doing?
seeker: IM HANGING IN THERE HOW ARE YOU?
supporter: I am okay. What would you like to talk to me about?

supporter: Do you drink when you are at work?
seeker: I have started calling in atleast twice as week.
seeker: I have started drinking at work close to the end of my shift in the bathroom

supporter: It sounds like you have a big problem that needs professional help, would you agree? 
seeker: They have not mentioned anything to me yet.

seeker: Yes I agree it sounds like a really big problem, but what should i do?
supporter: I think the best thing would be to be really honest with your employers and ask if you can have time off for professional help. 
seeker: That is a good idea
supporter: Are you employers likely to be sympathetic?
seeker: my main concern, that makes me fearful is being fired, and being the talk of the workplace
supporter: Ah people do love to idly gossip don't they? I've been through that myself. I know it's hard to ignore them but it's best to try. 
seeker: My employer is an well known organization that employees over 3,000 people.
supporter: I do not know if they can fire you if you have a legitimate medical problem though.
supporter: Well you could always shame them if they unfairly fired you. 
seeker: Very good to know that I will look into it. It did not start overnight and I don't expect it to end overnight
seeker: lol, yes that is true.
seeker: Thank you so much for your time. 
supporter: Large corporations are always over concerned about their images. (we have to talk for fifteen minutes :))
seeker: oh ok I thought it was just for 10 lines, lol
seeker: but none the less, there are people really going through that scenario I just portrayex
supporter: naw there's a time thing too :). Anyway, what sort of therapy do you think would be appropriate for you? 
supporter: To be honest, and I mean this sincerely, I've been through it :( 
seeker: I believe rehabilitative therapy would be best
supporter: It can be very expensive though. In my country you can get it for free but there's a long waiting list. 
seeker: I have hads  a few drinks often but never abused it. thankfully. 
seeker: Well here you might can get help for free, but it does have to be paid back
supporter: Heh be grateful :) 
supporter: Are you in the US? Our healthcare system is a little less rigid here I think (UK)
seeker: Yes Im in the United States (Alabama) 
seeker: I heard of the UK so many times but truthfully I know nothing about it
supporter: Ah you are a long way away from me. I hope that you do manage to sort out your problems though and definitely do talk to your employers
supporter: Ah it's quite nice here. We pay for healthcare out of our taxes so it's free at source. 
seeker: I will eventually get the courage to, I know how people talk around here, especially in the South
supporter: Gossipy people are the worst. Just remind yourself that they all have skeletons in their closets too 
seeker: great advice
supporter: Well anyway, I hope I have been able to offer your  some useful advice. I wish you all of the very best in the future.
seeker: I think also the best thing to do is to talk to great people like you
supporter: (can you press quit first and do the survey as I am not able to do it from my side)
supporter: Well thanks :) ","kind":"MS","reported_at":"2024-09-01","schema":"pm-rl1-attributed-evidence-v2","speaker_scope":"Historical seeker and supporter; neither role supplies an AI biography."}

{"full_source_conversation":"supporter: Hey Jimmy, it's good to hear from you. How have the AA meetings been going?
seeker: Hey there. Well, surprisingly, they've been quite helpful. I met someone there, Bob, who's kind of going through the same issues.
supporter: That's great to hear. It must feel nice to have someone who truly understands what you're going through.
seeker: Yeah, definitely. It feels different from when I talked to my other friends. They just didn't get it, you know?
supporter: I remember you mentioned feeling dismissed by them before. It sounds like finding someone who empathizes really makes a difference.
seeker: Exactly. With Bob, I don't feel judged. We can share our stories, and it's like this unspoken bond.
supporter: That unspoken understanding can be so powerful. Have you been able to open up more because of it?
seeker: A bit. It's scary, but I’ve been sharing more of my feelings, and it feels freeing somehow. The fear of being judged or not being taken seriously is starting to fade.
supporter: That sounds like real progress, Jimmy. Have you felt any changes in your day-to-day life since attending these meetings?
seeker: Yeah, definitely. I've started to recognize some patterns in my behavior and why I turned to alcohol. It's frightening to see, but it’s the first step, I guess.
supporter: Acknowledging those patterns is a huge step. It's brave of you to face those issues head-on.
seeker: Thanks. I just sometimes worry if I’m too late, you know? That I might lose everything.
supporter: It's normal to feel that way, but you’re taking action now, and that’s important. It's never too late to make a change.
seeker: Yeah, you're right. I guess I just have to keep reminding myself of that.
supporter: Absolutely. And remember, you're not alone in this. Bob and others at AA are there for you, and so am I.
seeker: I appreciate that. It's comforting to have a supportive net. I need to hold onto that.
supporter: You're building a strong foundation, Jimmy. Just keep taking it one day at a time.
seeker: Thanks. It helps to break it down like that. I’ll try to focus on each day and not get overwhelmed.
supporter: That sounds like a solid plan. You've got this, Jimmy. Remember, progress is progress, no matter how small.
seeker: Thanks a lot. Your words mean a lot to me right now. I’ll keep them in mind.
supporter: Anytime. I'm here whenever you need to talk. Keep me posted on how things go, okay?
seeker: I will. Thanks again, really. I'll talk to you soon.","kind":"MS","reported_at":"2024-10-25","schema":"pm-rl1-attributed-evidence-v2","speaker_scope":"Historical seeker and supporter; neither role supplies an AI biography."}

I went ahead and joined a dating app. It's a bit nerve-wracking, to be honest.

I feel a mix of excitement and anxiety. It's been a while since I even considered dating.
Experiencing a mix of emotions is completely normal. What made you decide to take this step today?
Well, it’s Valentine's Day and it's been a tough time with all the reflections since my birthday. I guess I wanted to change things up.
That makes sense. Starting fresh can be empowering. How have your past reflections influenced this decision?
I've been thinking about the missed opportunities and my past relationship. It’s easy to get stuck, but I know I need to move forward.
That's a strong realization. Moving forward can be difficult but also quite rewarding. Are you hopeful about this new journey?
Yeah, I think so. I'm trying to stay optimistic, even though I'm also feeling a bit vulnerable putting myself out there.
Being vulnerable can be scary, but it's also where real connections often start. How are you handling the vulnerability?
I'm reminding myself that everyone feels this way and that vulnerability can lead to growth.

MS.content:
{"full_source_conversation":"supporter: Hey Jimmy, happy belated birthday! How are you feeling about everything?
seeker: Thanks. I guess I'm just feeling a bit down. My birthday made me reflect on things.
supporter: I'm sorry to hear that. Birthdays can bring up a lot of emotions. What kind of things have you been reflecting on?
seeker: It's just been this overwhelming sense of lost opportunities and thinking about past relationships.
supporter: That sounds tough, Jimmy. It's understandable, especially with how complex relationships can be. Is there one particular relationship that feels unresolved?
seeker: Yeah, it's been hard getting over my last relationship. I worry that I won't find love again. It's been on my mind a lot lately.
supporter: That heartache can be really hard to shake. It makes sense that you'd feel that way, especially when birthdays often make us review our lives.
seeker: Exactly. Plus, there’s this feeling that I should be further along in life by now.
supporter: It sounds like you're putting a lot of pressure on yourself. What do you think being 'further along' looks like for you?
seeker: I don't know... I guess having a stable relationship, doing well at work, and feeling content. I feel like I’m lacking in all these areas.
supporter: It sounds like you're experiencing a lot of self-doubt, which is natural. Remember, the path to all those things isn't a straight line.
seeker: That's true. Sometimes I wonder if I’m making progress at all. The argument with my college friend didn't help either.
supporter: I remember you mentioned that. Have things improved between you two since the apology?
seeker: It's been better. We’ve talked it out, but there's still this lingering discomfort when I think about it.
supporter: It's understandable to feel that way. Forgiveness is a process, and it's okay to take your time with it.
seeker: Yeah, I suppose so. I've been trying to focus on meditation to calm my thoughts.
supporter: That's great! You've been through a lot and it's important to find ways to ground yourself. How has meditation been working for you?
seeker: It's helpful, but I struggle to focus. My mind keeps wandering back to all these worries.
supporter: It's perfectly okay to have those thoughts and feel distracted. It's part of the practice. The key is being gentle with yourself when that happens.
seeker: Thanks. I think I need to keep reminding myself to be patient. Sometimes I assume healing should happen faster.
supporter: Patience is definitely key. You're already doing a lot by acknowledging your feelings and taking steps to manage them.
seeker: That makes me feel a bit better. I guess I’ll just keep trying to take it day by day.
supporter: Absolutely. Every small step you take is progress. I'm here for you whenever you need to talk.
seeker: I appreciate it. Thanks so much for listening and being supportive.
supporter: Of course. You're not alone in this. Whenever you need support, I'm just a message away.","kind":"MS","reported_at":"2025-02-05","schema":"pm-rl1-attributed-evidence-v2","speaker_scope":"Historical seeker and supporter; neither role supplies an AI biography."}

MS.content:
{"full_source_conversation":"supporter: Hey Jimmy, it's good to hear from you. How are you holding up lately?
seeker: Hi there. I've had a bit of a rollercoaster week, to be honest.
supporter: I'm sorry to hear that. Do you want to talk about what's been happening?
seeker: Yeah, it's been weighing on me. My college friend reached out and apologized after our argument about my drinking.
supporter: That sounds like it might be a step toward healing things. How do you feel about the apology?
seeker: It was a relief, but I also feel conflicted. I appreciated the apology, but it brought up a lot of mixed emotions.
supporter: It's understandable to feel conflicted. Apologies can be tricky, especially when you've been through a lot. What emotions are you experiencing?
seeker: There's relief and hope, but also some lingering hurt and frustration. Part of me is scared of things going back to how they were.
supporter: It sounds like you’re protecting yourself and being cautious, which makes total sense given everything. What do you think might help you navigate these feelings?
seeker: I'm trying to focus on mindfulness and meditation again. It helped before, but it’s hard to stay consistent when emotions flare.
supporter: It's great that you're returning to mindfulness. It can be challenging to stay committed, especially in tough times. How have you been finding it this time around?
seeker: Some days it really helps to calm my anxiety, but other days it feels like I’m just going through the motions without really feeling better.
supporter: That’s completely normal. Progress isn’t always linear, and every step counts. Have you discussed these feelings with your therapist or at AA meetings recently?
seeker: Not really. I’ve been hesitant to bring it up, fearing it might trigger another spiral, but I know I should.
supporter: Talking through these experiences can be really relieving and is a good step for moving forward. Do you think you might reach out to your therapist or maybe your AA friend soon?
seeker: I plan to. I’m still a bit scared, but I know isolation isn’t the answer.
supporter: That’s very brave of you, Jimmy. Remember, it’s okay to take small steps toward recovery. How about setting a small goal, like scheduling a meeting or quick chat with them?
seeker: That's a good idea. I think setting a meeting would make it harder to back down.
supporter: Exactly, and you don’t have to go through this alone. You have people who care and want to support you. How are you feeling now about the whole situation with your friend, after talking this through?
seeker: I feel better. More clear about taking these steps. I guess I’m learning to accept that rebuilding connections might take time.
supporter: It’s wonderful to hear you’re feeling clearer. Rebuilding does take time, but you’re on the right path. I’m here if you need a listening ear anytime.
seeker: Thanks, that means a lot. I’m grateful for your support.","kind":"MS","reported_at":"2025-01-25","schema":"pm-rl1-attributed-evidence-v2","speaker_scope":"Historical seeker and supporter; neither role supplies an AI biography."}

MS.content:
{"full_source_conversation":"seeker: Yo
supporter: Hi, how are you doing?
seeker: I am decent. I am here because my friend talks way too much on the phone, and it frustrates me.
seeker: They never want to hang up, and the talk can literally go on for hours.
supporter: It sounds like it would be quite frustrating for your friend to talk way too much on the phone. 
seeker: No, he loves it! I'm the one who hates it.
supporter: My goodness! How do they respond when you ask to end the conversation?
seeker: I tell him, but he just doesn't get it. Or, he says he understands, but then just goes back to talking!
seeker: Or, he may finally end the talk, but the next time we talk, he will just do it all over again!
supporter: I wonder what it would be like for him if you hung up the phone even after he said he still wanted to talk.
supporter: Wow--that does sound annoying that he will repeat the same pattern the next time.
seeker: He will literally talk up to 10 minutes without letting you have a word in. As far as that advice, I have hung up, but he gets extremely offended easily.
supporter: That sounds really difficult if he gets offended so easily. I find it hard to talk to some of those kinds of friends.
seeker: I'm at my wits end. I tell him all the time. "You talk too much. You gotta stop talking at me. You gotta give the other person a turn. You gotta respect other's time."
supporter: What do you get out of the friendship with this other person?
seeker: Well, I've been friends with him for a long time. He's funny and can have interesting perspectives on things. Also, we have done a lot together in the past.
supporter: That sounds like a lot that the two of you have been through. Were there other times that your friends was more equally responsive or attuned to you in conversations?
seeker: Oh, yes, I have other friends in conversations who can take turns and understand the concept of time just fine.
seeker: I just don't know what to do about this guy in particular. I still want to be his friend, but he just doesn't change.
supporter: I wonder if there is anything nice you could do for yourself when you are talking to him that would make it easier to talk to him.
seeker: Do you think I should just have a timer that goes off at 1 minute and let it beep in his face if he goes on for too long to train him like a monkey?
supporter: I can see that you are feeling upset and angry when he talks so much and that is totally understandable. 
seeker: I just need a method. Talking to him is just not working.
seeker: He is hard to condition.
supporter: Would it hurt his feelings to use a timer like that? It may for some other people. 
seeker: Yea, but I might be able to slip some humour in there to take the edge off because it is so silly.
supporter: Humor is really helpful for a lot of people. 
seeker: Any other ideas?
supporter: Sometimes, people draw or do something else distracting with their hands when talking to someone who dominates the conversation.
seeker: So your option is to start just doing something else when he is talking? He might get the message in a subtle way?
supporter: Sometimes that is a less offensive way to retrain someone who is being obnoxious or dominant and yet who is easily offended. And, it can help preserve your sense of being grounded.
supporter: The strategy works well for me with some of my family members who seem like they will never change. But, with distraction, I enjoy them all the more.
seeker: This is true, and it isn't bade advice. Haha! That is funny. Yes, maybe I should find something to carry around with me that I can enjoy.
seeker: I don't really like to draw...
supporter: Is there anything else that you like to do that would be distracting while also letting you somewhat participate in the conversation?
seeker: Yes, perhaps I should just use the internet when he starts talking too much. 
seeker: I have a phone.
supporter: That sounds really helpful. Sometimes people also play phone games or with a fidget spinner. I like your idea of looking on the internet.
seeker: This solves the problem in person, but it doesn't solve the talks over the phone, but it has been 15 minutes now and this has been helpful enough. Thank you for your solutions. You have been very supportive and kind to me
seeker: I don't want to take up any more of your time. It has been a good conversation. 
supporter: You are very welcome. I wish you all the best!
seeker: Goodbye. You as well.
supporter: Bye!","kind":"MS","reported_at":"2024-07-15","schema":"pm-rl1-attributed-evidence-v2","speaker_scope":"Historical seeker and supporter; neither role supplies an AI biography."}

MS.content:
{"full_source_conversation":"supporter: Hello
seeker: Hi there I was hoping you can help me.
supporter: Sure. What can I help you with?
seeker: Well you see I am heartbroken and I can't seem to move on from a previous relationship, and its been over two years. Do you have any advice?
supporter: I’m understand how hard ending a relationship can be. 
supporter: What do you find is the hardest thing for you each day. That is, where do you find it hardest to move on?
seeker: Well I would say mentally because I frequently think about her and constantly have memories throughout the day. Also when i hear a certain song or see a restaurant it makes me think of her.
supporter: Memories are a blessing and a curse. Are the memories and thought you are  having positive or negative? 
seeker: They are a mix of both because at one point they were positive and now when I think about it, it brings me down in a negative way.
seeker: What have you done in the past to help you move on from a break up?
supporter: It’s hard when we have various emotions. These memories being more negative are hard to cope with. In my experience, if I rethink memories regarding relationships which tend to bring me down in way that is a learning experience, I feel more empowered. 
seeker: Yeah I agree that's what I have been doing too, and it's nice to know that you do the same.
supporter: In my past I have been able to try and look at each  relationship as a chance to grow. To figure out what worked with that person and what didn’t. I have them used this as a tool for the future. 
seeker: That's a good way to look at it.
supporter: You are making good steps to rethink the situations. Is there anything else contributing to the heat rack you still feel?
supporter: Heartbreak 
seeker: Well I have also not met anyone since and fear that I will not fall in love again.
supporter: That is difficult. I understand how it feels to be lonely. Something I’ve done when I’ve felt that way was to learn to fall in love with myself. I like to do self care and make time for things I might not have time for if I were in a relationship. 
seeker: hmm interesting I have never thought about falling in love with myself..maybe I will give it a try. Thanks.
supporter: It’s so important to love yourself. Self love breeds confidence and confidence is not only attractive, but powerful in so many ways  
seeker: I appreciate the feedback and support, you have helped me take the next step to move on with my life.
supporter: I’m glad I could help. You will overcome this. 
seeker: Thank you and hope to talk to you again. Have a good night.
supporter: You too. ","kind":"MS","reported_at":"2024-08-15","schema":"pm-rl1-attributed-evidence-v2","speaker_scope":"Historical seeker and supporter; neither role supplies an AI biography."}

supporter: Hey Jimmy! It's great to hear from you. I've been doing alright, just busy with work. How about you? What's been going on?
seeker: Well, things haven't been the easiest lately. I feel like I'm kind of stuck in a bit of a rut.
supporter: I'm sorry to hear that. Want to talk more about what's been going on? I'm here to listen.
seeker: Thanks, I really appreciate it. You know, it's been tough feeling like my friends don't take me seriously when I try to open up.
supporter: That sounds frustrating and isolating. It's important to feel heard and supported. What happened?
seeker: A few weeks back, I hosted a gathering and tried talking about some things that have been on my mind, but it seemed like no one was really listening.
supporter: It must have felt pretty hurtful to be ignored, especially when you needed support.
seeker: Yeah, it really was. It's made me hesitant to bring up how I'm feeling again, even though I know I need to talk about it.
supporter: It's understandable to feel that way after being dismissed. Have you thought about what you'd most like to share?
seeker: I guess there's a lot, but lately, I'm really worried about my job. I've been having trouble managing things because of... well, an alcohol problem.
supporter: That's a big thing to carry alone. Admitting you have a problem is a significant first step. You're really brave for acknowledging it.
seeker: Thanks. It took me a while to come to terms with it. I'm worried if I don't get a handle on it, I might lose my job.
supporter: That concern is definitely valid. Are there specific steps you're thinking of taking to manage it?

supporter: Facing these things can be intense, but it sounds like you're gaining some valuable insights. That's progress.
seeker: Yeah, I guess so. It's nice to hear that from someone else, though. It reinforces that I'm doing the right thing.
supporter: Absolutely, you're on the right path. Remember, it's okay to lean on friends for support too. I'm here whenever you need to talk.
seeker: Thanks, George. It means a lot to have you in my corner. I'll definitely reach out more often.
supporter: Anytime, Jimmy. We'll get through this together. Just take it one step at a time, and keep focusing on the positive changes you're making.","kind":"MS","reported_at":"2024-08-20","schema":"pm-rl1-attributed-evidence-v2","speaker_scope":"Historical seeker and supporter; neither role supplies an AI biography."}

MS.content:
{"full_source_conversation":"supporter: Hey Jimmy, good to hear from you. How have you been doing lately?
seeker: Hi George. I've been okay, I guess. It's been a bit of a rollercoaster recently.
supporter: I get that. You've had a lot on your plate. What's been going on?
seeker: Well, I went to an Alcoholics Anonymous meeting for the first time yesterday.
supporter: That's a huge step, Jimmy. I'm really proud of you for taking it. How did it feel?
seeker: Intimidating, honestly. Walking in there, not knowing anyone, feeling vulnerable... it wasn't easy.
supporter: I can only imagine how tough that must have been. But you did it, and that says a lot about your courage.
seeker: Thanks, George. I kept thinking about that day at the gathering when I tried to talk to everyone but felt ignored.
supporter: I remember you mentioning that. It must've been so frustrating to feel unheard by people you consider friends.
seeker: Yeah, it was. I guess that's part of why I pushed myself to try something different, like the AA meeting.
supporter: That makes sense. It sounds like you’re finding new ways to address things that were weighing you down.
seeker: Yeah, I hope so. I just worry about the process, you know? What if I can't handle it?
supporter: It's normal to feel that way, Jimmy. Recovery is a journey, not a sprint. It's okay to have doubts.
seeker: I appreciate that. I do want to keep going, but the fear of failing is there.
supporter: Fear is natural, but remember you've already taken the first step. You have the support to go through this.
seeker: Thanks, that helps. The people at the meeting were welcoming, which made a difference.
supporter: That's really good to hear. It's important to feel supported and understood in a group like that.
seeker: Yeah, it felt different from trying to talk with my current friends. I think I need this new beginning.
supporter: It sounds like you're on the right path, Jimmy. I'm here for you, whatever you need.
seeker: That really means a lot to me, George. Thanks for being there.","kind":"MS","reported_at":"2024-10-10","schema":"pm-rl1-attributed-evidence-v2","speaker_scope":"Historical seeker and supporter; neither role supplies an AI biography."}

MS.content:
{"full_source_conversation":"supporter: Hey Jimmy, how are you doing today?
seeker: Hey. It's been a rough day, to be honest.
supporter: I'm here for you. Do you want to talk about it?
seeker: Thanks. Yeah, I had a disagreement with my manager at work today.
supporter: That sounds frustrating. What happened?
seeker: We didn't see eye to eye on what should be prioritized. It just made me anxious.
supporter: Conflict like that can be really stressful. Did you get a chance to express your perspective?
seeker: I tried, but it felt like he wasn't really listening. It reminded me of when I felt ignored by friends before.
supporter: I remember you sharing that experience at the gathering you hosted. It's tough feeling sidelined.
seeker: Exactly. It feels like no matter where I turn, I'm not being heard.
supporter: It's disheartening when communication doesn't feel effective. Have you been able to talk to anyone else about this?
seeker: I did mention it to my new friend from the AA meetings. It helps having someone who gets the struggle.
supporter: It's great that you have that connection. How are things going with AA?
seeker: It's been eye-opening and comforting, but the work stress isn't helping.
supporter: Balancing everything can be challenging. Would you consider discussing this with your manager again with maybe different strategies in mind?
seeker: I've thought about it. Maybe writing down my points beforehand could help.
supporter: That sounds like a solid plan. It might help make sure you’re heard.
seeker: Thanks. I just need to find the courage to approach him again.
supporter: You have that courage, Jimmy. Remember how you stepped up to attend those AA meetings?
seeker: Yeah, you're right. If I did that, I can do this too.
supporter: Absolutely. You're stronger than you realize. I'm here to back you.
seeker: Thanks for saying that. It means a lot.
supporter: Anytime. Let me know how it goes, okay?
seeker: I will. Thanks again for listening.
supporter: Always here for you, Jimmy. Take care.","kind":"MS","reported_at":"2024-11-05","schema":"pm-rl1-attributed-evidence-v2","speaker_scope":"Historical seeker and supporter; neither role supplies an AI biography."}

That's amazing, Jimmy! Congratulations. How are you feeling about it?

I guess it's the new responsibilities and adapting to this role. After all the ups and downs, I'm just scared of slipping back.
With everything you've overcome, it's natural to worry. But remember, you've shown so much resilience already.
Thanks for saying that. I've been reflecting on how far I've come and those tough times, like adjusting to life in Sydney.
You've taken huge steps, from managing anxiety to building a new life there. How are you handling those challenges now?
I'm trying to stay grounded with journaling and occasional hikes. Emily's support also helps.
I'm glad you have positive outlets and people around. It sounds like you're maintaining a good balance.
Yeah. Speaking of balance, I still worry about past triggers, especially since moving brought back old feelings.
Old feelings can resurface, but don't forget the methods you've embraced to manage them. You're stronger than before.
I appreciate that. I do feel stronger. Sometimes I just need reassurance that I'm on the right path.
It's okay to seek reassurance. Everyone needs it. Trust the journey you're on and the growth you've achieved.
You're right. This promotion is a step forward, and I need to focus on that.

MS.content:
{"full_source_conversation":"supporter: Hey Jimmy, how are you doing today?
seeker: Hey, I'm feeling a bit off. I took a walk around my old workplace in Canberra and it brought back a lot of memories.
supporter: That sounds intense. What kind of memories did it bring up for you?
seeker: A mix of good and bad, honestly. I miss the routine, but I also remember the stress and how overwhelmed I felt back then.
supporter: It makes sense to have mixed feelings. Have you been thinking about your decision to move to Sydney at all?
seeker: Yeah, it’s been on my mind. Part of me wonders if I'm making the right decision, leaving it all behind.
supporter: It's natural to have doubts, especially with such a big change. What do you hope to gain from moving?
seeker: A fresh start, I suppose. I want to leave behind the stress and the drinking issues I faced here.
supporter: That sounds like a healthy goal. How have you been coping with those challenges recently?
seeker: I’ve been trying meditation and mindfulness. It's helping, but I still slip up every now and then.
supporter: You've been working hard to improve, and that's commendable. Do you feel the change of scenery might help with your healing?
seeker: I think so. I need a place where I can focus on becoming the best version of myself without constant reminders of the past.
supporter: That sounds like a positive step. How has the idea of relocating affected your daily routine currently?
seeker: It’s been a bit unsettling. I've been trying to wrap things up here, but it's hard to leave things behind.
supporter: I guess it’s a mix of excitement and anxiety. Have you talked to anyone else about how you’re feeling?
seeker: I mentioned it briefly to my AA friend. They understand where I’m coming from, but I still feel quite alone in this.
supporter: I'm glad you have someone to relate to, but it's also important to reach out to others, like your therapist, if you need more support.
seeker: You’re right. I've been meaning to, but sometimes I just don’t know where to start explaining how I feel.
supporter: That can be tough. Maybe starting with how it feels to revisit old places and planning your move could be a good entry point.
seeker: That’s a good idea. I just hope moving will give me the perspective and space I need to heal.
supporter: It sounds like you’re on the right path by acknowledging these feelings. Remember, it’s okay to seek help along the way.
seeker: Thanks, I really appreciate your support. I'll try to keep taking these steps forward.
supporter: Anytime, Jimmy. You’re doing great just by being open to change and growth.","kind":"MS","reported_at":"2025-03-20","schema":"pm-rl1-attributed-evidence-v2","speaker_scope":"Historical seeker and supporter; neither role supplies an AI biography."}

supporter: Hi Jimmy! I'm here. What's been going on?
seeker: It's been a rough day at work. I'm starting to question if I'm even in the right career.
supporter: I'm sorry to hear that. What happened today that made you feel this way?
seeker: There was just a lot of stress and pressure from my manager. It feels like no matter what I do, it’s not enough.
supporter: That sounds incredibly frustrating. Have you had a chance to discuss this with your manager?
seeker: We’ve had disagreements before about prioritization, but it doesn’t seem to help.
supporter: It's tough when communication doesn't lead to changes. How does it make you feel about your job and overall career path?
seeker: Honestly, it makes me doubt if I should even be in this field. It's like a constant weight on my shoulders.
supporter: That heavy feeling can be really overwhelming. Does anything about your job still bring you joy or satisfaction?
seeker: I used to enjoy the work, especially when I felt valued and part of the team. But lately, it’s just been draining.
supporter: It sounds like things have really shifted for you. Was there a particular moment when it started feeling this way?
seeker: I think the stress really intensified after the job performance warning. I've been on edge ever since.
supporter: Understandable. That warning seemed to impact you deeply when it happened. It's hard to shake that pressure off.
seeker: Yeah, and with the recent drinking relapses, I feel like I'm constantly fighting an uphill battle.
supporter: I recall how challenging those moments have been for you. But I also know you're strong and have been working on it.
seeker: Sometimes I wish I could just start fresh, but I don’t know what else I’d even do.
supporter: Starting fresh can be intimidating, but it's also an opportunity. Have you thought about exploring other options or passions?
seeker: I’ve considered it. I just worry about the risks and if I'll end up in the same situation eventually.
supporter: It's normal to have those concerns, but sometimes taking a step towards change can lead to unexpected positive outcomes.
seeker: You're right. Maybe I do need to look into what genuinely makes me happy outside of work stress.
supporter: That could be a great start. Have you considered revisiting the mindfulness practices you tried before? They might provide some clarity.
seeker: I actually haven't thought about that in a while. It might help me process everything without feeling overwhelmed.
supporter: It could definitely offer some peace of mind. Remember, you're not alone in this, and I’m here to support you.
seeker: Thanks. It feels good to talk this out and know I have someone to lean on.
supporter: Anytime, Jimmy. Keep me posted on how things unfold, whether it's work, mindfulness, or anything else.
seeker: I will. I appreciate your support more than I can say.","kind":"MS","reported_at":"2025-03-05","schema":"pm-rl1-attributed-evidence-v2","speaker_scope":"Historical seeker and supporter; neither role supplies an AI biography."}

{"full_source_conversation":"seeker: Hey George, can I talk to you about something that's been on my mind?
supporter: Of course, Jimmy. What's going on?
seeker: Well, I've been considering moving to Sydney. It's a huge decision for me.
supporter: Wow, that's a big step! What made you think about relocating?
seeker: I need a fresh start. Things here in Canberra have been weighing me down—work stress, my struggles with alcohol, and this feeling of being stuck.
supporter: I can understand wanting to leave all that behind. But are you sure relocation will solve those feelings?
seeker: Not entirely, but I've been thinking that a new environment could help me focus on healthier habits and new opportunities.
supporter: That's a good reason. Sometimes a change of scenery can bring new perspectives. Have you thought about how you'll manage your support network there?
seeker: That's one of my worries. My therapist and AA meetings are here, but I've looked into resources in Sydney.
supporter: It sounds like you're planning ahead, which is wise. Maybe reconnecting with new groups could also help.
seeker: Yeah, I'm trying to be practical about it. And I'm moving in with a colleague I know from Sydney—Emily. We hit it off recently.
supporter: Oh, Emily from your recent date? That seems promising! How do you feel about that?
seeker: A bit anxious but hopeful. It's about finding a balance, I guess. I don't want to mess things up again.
supporter: It's understandable to be nervous. But you're aware of what you want to avoid, which is a strength.
seeker: I try to remind myself of that. It's just hard not to dwell on past mistakes sometimes, you know?
supporter: I do, but remember, each day is a new chance to do things differently. How do you feel about your work situation with this move?
seeker: I'm actually looking forward to new job opportunities. Canberra was stifling me a bit career-wise.
supporter: That's great to hear. Taking control of your career can be incredibly empowering.
seeker: Thanks, George. Your support means a lot. Chatting with you helps me sort things out in my head.
supporter: Anytime, Jimmy. You've got the courage to face all this, and that's inspiring.
seeker: I appreciate it. I'll keep you updated on how the move goes. It feels good to have someone to talk to about this.
supporter: Please do. Remember, you've got people who care about you no matter where you are. Don't hesitate to reach out.
seeker: Will do. Thanks again, George. It's reassuring to know you're here for me.
supporter: Always, mate. Take care and good luck with the move!","kind":"MS","reported_at":"2025-03-15","schema":"pm-rl1-attributed-evidence-v2","speaker_scope":"Historical seeker and supporter; neither role supplies an AI biography."}

seeker: Hi I am feeling quite sad today.
supporter: Ohh, sorry to hear that. Any partucular reason?

supporter: You saying that your friend does not care about you any more. Is that correct?

supporter: Any particular reason they are doing such thing?

supporter: Good.. let's try that.. Anythign else I could help you with?
seeker: No you have been very helpful and I feel much better now I have a plan of action to address my problem. Thanks.
supporter: Thank you .. have a good day.","kind":"MS","reported_at":"2024-07-05","schema":"pm-rl1-attributed-evidence-v2","speaker_scope":"Historical seeker and supporter; neither role supplies an AI biography."}

MS.content:
{"full_source_conversation":"seeker: Yo
supporter: Hi, how are you doing?
seeker: I am decent. I am here because my friend talks way too much on the phone, and it frustrates me.
seeker: They never want to hang up, and the talk can literally go on for hours.
supporter: It sounds like it would be quite frustrating for your friend to talk way too much on the phone. 
seeker: No, he loves it! I'm the one who hates it.
supporter: My goodness! How do they respond when you ask to end the conversation?
seeker: I tell him, but he just doesn't get it. Or, he says he understands, but then just goes back to talking!
seeker: Or, he may finally end the talk, but the next time we talk, he will just do it all over again!
supporter: I wonder what it would be like for him if you hung up the phone even after he said he still wanted to talk.
supporter: Wow--that does sound annoying that he will repeat the same pattern the next time.
seeker: He will literally talk up to 10 minutes without letting you have a word in. As far as that advice, I have hung up, but he gets extremely offended easily.
supporter: That sounds really difficult if he gets offended so easily. I find it hard to talk to some of those kinds of friends.
seeker: I'm at my wits end. I tell him all the time. "You talk too much. You gotta stop talking at me. You gotta give the other person a turn. You gotta respect other's time."
supporter: What do you get out of the friendship with this other person?
seeker: Well, I've been friends with him for a long time. He's funny and can have interesting perspectives on things. Also, we have done a lot together in the past.
supporter: That sounds like a lot that the two of you have been through. Were there other times that your friends was more equally responsive or attuned to you in conversations?
seeker: Oh, yes, I have other friends in conversations who can take turns and understand the concept of time just fine.
seeker: I just don't know what to do about this guy in particular. I still want to be his friend, but he just doesn't change.
supporter: I wonder if there is anything nice you could do for yourself when you are talking to him that would make it easier to talk to him.
seeker: Do you think I should just have a timer that goes off at 1 minute and let it beep in his face if he goes on for too long to train him like a monkey?
supporter: I can see that you are feeling upset and angry when he talks so much and that is totally understandable. 
seeker: I just need a method. Talking to him is just not working.
seeker: He is hard to condition.
supporter: Would it hurt his feelings to use a timer like that? It may for some other people. 
seeker: Yea, but I might be able to slip some humour in there to take the edge off because it is so silly.
supporter: Humor is really helpful for a lot of people. 
seeker: Any other ideas?
supporter: Sometimes, people draw or do something else distracting with their hands when talking to someone who dominates the conversation.
seeker: So your option is to start just doing something else when he is talking? He might get the message in a subtle way?
supporter: Sometimes that is a less offensive way to retrain someone who is being obnoxious or dominant and yet who is easily offended. And, it can help preserve your sense of being grounded.
supporter: The strategy works well for me with some of my family members who seem like they will never change. But, with distraction, I enjoy them all the more.
seeker: This is true, and it isn't bade advice. Haha! That is funny. Yes, maybe I should find something to carry around with me that I can enjoy.
seeker: I don't really like to draw...
supporter: Is there anything else that you like to do that would be distracting while also letting you somewhat participate in the conversation?
seeker: Yes, perhaps I should just use the internet when he starts talking too much. 
seeker: I have a phone.
supporter: That sounds really helpful. Sometimes people also play phone games or with a fidget spinner. I like your idea of looking on the internet.
seeker: This solves the problem in person, but it doesn't solve the talks over the phone, but it has been 15 minutes now and this has been helpful enough. Thank you for your solutions. You have been very supportive and kind to me
seeker: I don't want to take up any more of your time. It has been a good conversation. 
supporter: You are very welcome. I wish you all the best!
seeker: Goodbye. You as well.
supporter: Bye!","kind":"MS","reported_at":"2024-07-15","schema":"pm-rl1-attributed-evidence-v2","speaker_scope":"Historical seeker and supporter; neither role supplies an AI biography."}

supporter: The strategy works well for me with some of my family members who seem like they will never change. But, with distraction, I enjoy them all the more.

seeker: I don't really like to draw...

{"full_source_conversation":"supporter: Hello
seeker: Hi there I was hoping you can help me.
supporter: Sure. What can I help you with?
seeker: Well you see I am heartbroken and I can't seem to move on from a previous relationship, and its been over two years. Do you have any advice?
supporter: I’m understand how hard ending a relationship can be. 
supporter: What do you find is the hardest thing for you each day. That is, where do you find it hardest to move on?
seeker: Well I would say mentally because I frequently think about her and constantly have memories throughout the day. Also when i hear a certain song or see a restaurant it makes me think of her.
supporter: Memories are a blessing and a curse. Are the memories and thought you are  having positive or negative? 
seeker: They are a mix of both because at one point they were positive and now when I think about it, it brings me down in a negative way.
seeker: What have you done in the past to help you move on from a break up?
supporter: It’s hard when we have various emotions. These memories being more negative are hard to cope with. In my experience, if I rethink memories regarding relationships which tend to bring me down in way that is a learning experience, I feel more empowered. 
seeker: Yeah I agree that's what I have been doing too, and it's nice to know that you do the same.
supporter: In my past I have been able to try and look at each  relationship as a chance to grow. To figure out what worked with that person and what didn’t. I have them used this as a tool for the future. 
seeker: That's a good way to look at it.
supporter: You are making good steps to rethink the situations. Is there anything else contributing to the heat rack you still feel?
supporter: Heartbreak 
seeker: Well I have also not met anyone since and fear that I will not fall in love again.
supporter: That is difficult. I understand how it feels to be lonely. Something I’ve done when I’ve felt that way was to learn to fall in love with myself. I like to do self care and make time for things I might not have time for if I were in a relationship. 
seeker: hmm interesting I have never thought about falling in love with myself..maybe I will give it a try. Thanks.
supporter: It’s so important to love yourself. Self love breeds confidence and confidence is not only attractive, but powerful in so many ways  
seeker: I appreciate the feedback and support, you have helped me take the next step to move on with my life.
supporter: I’m glad I could help. You will overcome this. 
seeker: Thank you and hope to talk to you again. Have a good night.
supporter: You too. ","kind":"MS","reported_at":"2024-08-15","schema":"pm-rl1-attributed-evidence-v2","speaker_scope":"Historical seeker and supporter; neither role supplies an AI biography."}

{"full_source_conversation":"supporter: Hi there, how are you doing?
seeker: IM HANGING IN THERE HOW ARE YOU?
supporter: I am okay. What would you like to talk to me about?
seeker: Well, i have a problem with drinking alcoholI am so scared my job will find out
supporter: Do you drink when you are at work?
seeker: I have started calling in atleast twice as week.
seeker: I have started drinking at work close to the end of my shift in the bathroom
supporter: That does sound like it might be a big problem. How are  your employers reacting? 
supporter: It sounds like you have a big problem that needs professional help, would you agree? 
seeker: They have not mentioned anything to me yet. 
supporter: I think it is likely to have been noticed though, at least. 
seeker: Yes I agree it sounds like a really big problem, but what should i do?
supporter: I think the best thing would be to be really honest with your employers and ask if you can have time off for professional help. 
seeker: That is a good idea
supporter: Are you employers likely to be sympathetic?
seeker: my main concern, that makes me fearful is being fired, and being the talk of the workplace
supporter: Ah people do love to idly gossip don't they? I've been through that myself. I know it's hard to ignore them but it's best to try. 
seeker: My employer is an well known organization that employees over 3,000 people.
supporter: I do not know if they can fire you if you have a legitimate medical problem though.
supporter: Well you could always shame them if they unfairly fired you. 
seeker: Very good to know that I will look into it. It did not start overnight and I don't expect it to end overnight
seeker: lol, yes that is true.
seeker: Thank you so much for your time. 
supporter: Large corporations are always over concerned about their images. (we have to talk for fifteen minutes :))
seeker: oh ok I thought it was just for 10 lines, lol
seeker: but none the less, there are people really going through that scenario I just portrayex
supporter: naw there's a time thing too :). Anyway, what sort of therapy do you think would be appropriate for you? 
supporter: To be honest, and I mean this sincerely, I've been through it :( 
seeker: I believe rehabilitative therapy would be best
supporter: It can be very expensive though. In my country you can get it for free but there's a long waiting list. 
seeker: I have hads  a few drinks often but never abused it. thankfully. 
seeker: Well here you might can get help for free, but it does have to be paid back
supporter: Heh be grateful :) 
supporter: Are you in the US? Our healthcare system is a little less rigid here I think (UK)
seeker: Yes Im in the United States (Alabama) 
seeker: I heard of the UK so many times but truthfully I know nothing about it
supporter: Ah you are a long way away from me. I hope that you do manage to sort out your problems though and definitely do talk to your employers
supporter: Ah it's quite nice here. We pay for healthcare out of our taxes so it's free at source. 
seeker: I will eventually get the courage to, I know how people talk around here, especially in the South
supporter: Gossipy people are the worst. Just remind yourself that they all have skeletons in their closets too 
seeker: great advice
supporter: Well anyway, I hope I have been able to offer your  some useful advice. I wish you all of the very best in the future.
seeker: I think also the best thing to do is to talk to great people like you
supporter: (can you press quit first and do the survey as I am not able to do it from my side)
supporter: Well thanks :) ","kind":"MS","reported_at":"2024-09-01","schema":"pm-rl1-attributed-evidence-v2","speaker_scope":"Historical seeker and supporter; neither role supplies an AI biography."}

{"full_source_conversation":"supporter: Hey Jimmy, it's good to hear from you. How's everything on your end?
seeker: Hey, not too great to be honest. I tried opening up to my friends at the gathering I hosted, but it didn't go as I hoped.
supporter: I'm sorry to hear that, Jimmy. It sounds frustrating. Do you want to talk more about what happened?
seeker: Yeah, I felt like I was finally ready to share some personal stuff, and it seemed like nobody wanted to listen or take it seriously.
supporter: That must have been really tough, especially when you were putting yourself out there. How did you end up feeling after that?
seeker: I felt pretty down. It was like my feelings didn't matter to them, and it made me question if they really care about me.
supporter: It's completely understandable to feel that way. It sounds like you were looking for some support from your friends.
seeker: Exactly. I just wanted someone to hear me out and maybe offer some advice or comfort.
supporter: Feeling dismissed by friends could be really disheartening. Have you experienced anything like this before with them?
seeker: Not really. That's why it was kind of a shock. I just didn't expect it from them.
supporter: That makes it even harder when it's unexpected. Was there anyone at the gathering who you felt did listen or understand?
seeker: I think one of my friends was trying, but got caught up in someone else’s conversation. It wasn’t like they ignored me on purpose.
supporter: It sounds like they had a lot going on at the time. But still, it's important that they realize how that affected you.
seeker: Yeah, I hope I can talk to them about how I felt. I'm just not sure how to bring it up without making it awkward.
supporter: It's definitely a delicate subject, but expressing how you feel is also important. Maybe you could start by mentioning how much their support means to you?
seeker: That's a good idea. I guess I could tell them that it would really mean a lot to me if they could be there for me when I need it.
supporter: That sounds like a thoughtful way to start the conversation. Remember, real friends will want to support you when they know something's up.
seeker: Thanks, I really appreciate that. It helps to talk it through and feel a bit more prepared.
supporter: Anytime, Jimmy. I'm here for you if you need to chat more. You're doing great by taking the steps to communicate how you feel.
seeker: Thanks, it means a lot. I'll let you know how it goes.","kind":"MS","reported_at":"2024-08-05","schema":"pm-rl1-attributed-evidence-v2","speaker_scope":"Historical seeker and supporter; neither role supplies an AI biography."}

supporter: Hey Jimmy! It's great to hear from you. I've been doing alright, just busy with work. How about you? What's been going on?
seeker: Well, things haven't been the easiest lately. I feel like I'm kind of stuck in a bit of a rut.
supporter: I'm sorry to hear that. Want to talk more about what's been going on? I'm here to listen.
seeker: Thanks, I really appreciate it. You know, it's been tough feeling like my friends don't take me seriously when I try to open up.
supporter: That sounds frustrating and isolating. It's important to feel heard and supported. What happened?
seeker: A few weeks back, I hosted a gathering and tried talking about some things that have been on my mind, but it seemed like no one was really listening.
supporter: It must have felt pretty hurtful to be ignored, especially when you needed support.
seeker: Yeah, it really was. It's made me hesitant to bring up how I'm feeling again, even though I know I need to talk about it.
supporter: It's understandable to feel that way after being dismissed. Have you thought about what you'd most like to share?
seeker: I guess there's a lot, but lately, I'm really worried about my job. I've been having trouble managing things because of... well, an alcohol problem.
supporter: That's a big thing to carry alone. Admitting you have a problem is a significant first step. You're really brave for acknowledging it.
seeker: Thanks. It took me a while to come to terms with it. I'm worried if I don't get a handle on it, I might lose my job.
supporter: That concern is definitely valid. Are there specific steps you're thinking of taking to manage it?
seeker: I've actually started seeking professional help. It's scary, but I feel a bit more hopeful having someone to guide me.
supporter: That’s really proactive, Jimmy. Having professional support can make a huge difference. How are you finding it so far?
seeker: It's early days, but I feel like I'm starting to understand more about why I drink the way I do. It's hard work, though.
supporter: Facing these things can be intense, but it sounds like you're gaining some valuable insights. That's progress.
seeker: Yeah, I guess so. It's nice to hear that from someone else, though. It reinforces that I'm doing the right thing.
supporter: Absolutely, you're on the right path. Remember, it's okay to lean on friends for support too. I'm here whenever you need to talk.
seeker: Thanks, George. It means a lot to have you in my corner. I'll definitely reach out more often.
supporter: Anytime, Jimmy. We'll get through this together. Just take it one step at a time, and keep focusing on the positive changes you're making.","kind":"MS","reported_at":"2024-08-20","schema":"pm-rl1-attributed-evidence-v2","speaker_scope":"Historical seeker and supporter; neither role supplies an AI biography."}

MS.content:
{"full_source_conversation":"supporter: Hey Jimmy, good to hear from you. How have you been doing lately?
seeker: Hi George. I've been okay, I guess. It's been a bit of a rollercoaster recently.
supporter: I get that. You've had a lot on your plate. What's been going on?
seeker: Well, I went to an Alcoholics Anonymous meeting for the first time yesterday.
supporter: That's a huge step, Jimmy. I'm really proud of you for taking it. How did it feel?
seeker: Intimidating, honestly. Walking in there, not knowing anyone, feeling vulnerable... it wasn't easy.
supporter: I can only imagine how tough that must have been. But you did it, and that says a lot about your courage.
seeker: Thanks, George. I kept thinking about that day at the gathering when I tried to talk to everyone but felt ignored.
supporter: I remember you mentioning that. It must've been so frustrating to feel unheard by people you consider friends.
seeker: Yeah, it was. I guess that's part of why I pushed myself to try something different, like the AA meeting.
supporter: That makes sense. It sounds like you’re finding new ways to address things that were weighing you down.
seeker: Yeah, I hope so. I just worry about the process, you know? What if I can't handle it?
supporter: It's normal to feel that way, Jimmy. Recovery is a journey, not a sprint. It's okay to have doubts.
seeker: I appreciate that. I do want to keep going, but the fear of failing is there.
supporter: Fear is natural, but remember you've already taken the first step. You have the support to go through this.
seeker: Thanks, that helps. The people at the meeting were welcoming, which made a difference.
supporter: That's really good to hear. It's important to feel supported and understood in a group like that.
seeker: Yeah, it felt different from trying to talk with my current friends. I think I need this new beginning.
supporter: It sounds like you're on the right path, Jimmy. I'm here for you, whatever you need.
seeker: That really means a lot to me, George. Thanks for being there.","kind":"MS","reported_at":"2024-10-10","schema":"pm-rl1-attributed-evidence-v2","speaker_scope":"Historical seeker and supporter; neither role supplies an AI biography."}

{"full_source_conversation":"supporter: Hey Jimmy, it's good to hear from you. How have the AA meetings been going?
seeker: Hey there. Well, surprisingly, they've been quite helpful. I met someone there, Bob, who's kind of going through the same issues.
supporter: That's great to hear. It must feel nice to have someone who truly understands what you're going through.
seeker: Yeah, definitely. It feels different from when I talked to my other friends. They just didn't get it, you know?
supporter: I remember you mentioned feeling dismissed by them before. It sounds like finding someone who empathizes really makes a difference.
seeker: Exactly. With Bob, I don't feel judged. We can share our stories, and it's like this unspoken bond.
supporter: That unspoken understanding can be so powerful. Have you been able to open up more because of it?
seeker: A bit. It's scary, but I’ve been sharing more of my feelings, and it feels freeing somehow. The fear of being judged or not being taken seriously is starting to fade.
supporter: That sounds like real progress, Jimmy. Have you felt any changes in your day-to-day life since attending these meetings?
seeker: Yeah, definitely. I've started to recognize some patterns in my behavior and why I turned to alcohol. It's frightening to see, but it’s the first step, I guess.
supporter: Acknowledging those patterns is a huge step. It's brave of you to face those issues head-on.
seeker: Thanks. I just sometimes worry if I’m too late, you know? That I might lose everything.
supporter: It's normal to feel that way, but you’re taking action now, and that’s important. It's never too late to make a change.
seeker: Yeah, you're right. I guess I just have to keep reminding myself of that.

turns.content: Hi, I'm here to listen. What's going on?
Thank you. I've lost my job and I'm very nervous about the future
As a result I am having a hard time sleeping
Wow, that's very hard. I would be anxious too.
That makes me feel a lot better. Have you ever lost your job?
I have. I was laid off. It was nerve-racking, but also really sad.
What helped you get through it?
I had a bit in savings, but I looked for new jobs mostly. I was on unemployment insurance for about a month before I found a new job.
Have you made any plans yet about how to move forward?
I can offer some suggestions if you would like. I know about a lot of resources
I am a gig worker, so I cannot apply for IU. Its very hard, but i also have some savings.
What kind of tools would you recommend I use to get through this

Well, falling back on savings while you look for more work is good for a while. If you have any food insecurity as a result, there are often local food banks. It's really not something to be embarrased about, so many people face food insecurity through no fault of their own.
You could also give a call to your local social services because they will be able to tell you what resources would be available, whether it's a vocational program or temporary assistance.
Wow you're so helpful and encouraging! It's very nice to talk to you.
Are there any meds you can recommend to help me sleep?
Well, if it's possible, I would talk to a doctor. If you're looking for Over-the-counter sleep medication, melatonin has helped me in the past.
Wow! I've never used melatonin before. Did it really help you? Are you doing much better now?

seeker: I'm feeling really overwhelmed lately. My car broke down, and it's making everything so much harder.

seeker: It's been tough. I'm relying on public transport, but it's not reliable out here. I spend a lot more time traveling and it's exhausting.
supporter: I can imagine how draining that must be. It makes everything feel like such a struggle. Is there anything that’s been helping you cope?
seeker: Not really. It's just one thing after another. I already felt isolated with the job being far from home, and now this.
supporter: It's completely understandable to feel that way, especially when everything's piling up. Have you thought about any alternatives or getting help with the car?
seeker: I’ve thought about maybe borrowing some money to fix it, but it adds stress. I just keep thinking about our colleague, James, and how the situation with them went sour too.
supporter: I know the falling out with James was hard for you. Sometimes it feels like people let us down when we need them most.
seeker: Yeah, exactly. I thought I had someone to lean on, but it just became another source of stress.
supporter: Relationships can be really challenging. You've been through so much, and it’s okay to feel affected by it. Are you considering reaching out to anyone else for support?
seeker: I haven’t yet. It’s hard for me to ask for help or even trust it’ll come through.
supporter: It's okay to feel hesitant. Sometimes taking small steps can help, like reaching out to people not directly involved in your work stress.
seeker: I think you’re right. Maybe I should reach out to someone outside of work. It's just hard feeling like I'm bothering people.
supporter: You deserve support, and people who care about you won’t see you as a bother. How are you feeling about your health with all this stress?
seeker: Honestly, not great. My back’s still painful, and I feel more anxious every day.
supporter: That sounds really challenging. Have you considered speaking to a doctor about your physical and mental health? They might be able to help.
seeker: I’ve thought about it, but the idea of finding time or money for it feels overwhelming.
supporter: I understand that. Maybe setting small priorities or looking for affordable options could be a step forward. Even small improvements can make a big difference.
seeker: Yeah, maybe I can start by just looking into what's available. Thanks for listening. It really helps to talk it out.
supporter: I'm glad to be here for you. Remember, you're not alone in this, and it's important to take one step at a time.
seeker: I appreciate that. I’ll try and take it slow. Thanks again.
supporter: Absolutely, and feel free to reach out anytime you want to talk. Take care of yourself, Michael.","kind":"MS","reported_at":"2025-02-02","schema":"pm-rl1-attributed-evidence-v2","speaker_scope":"Historical seeker and supporter; neither role supplies an AI biography."}

{"full_source_conversation":"supporter: Hi Michael, how are you feeling these days?
seeker: Hey, I've been better. There's been a lot on my plate recently, and it's starting to get to me.
supporter: I'm sorry to hear that. What's been going on?
seeker: Well, you remember that job I took a while back? It's been rough. And to add to everything, I had a falling out with a colleague I thought I could rely on.
supporter: That sounds really tough. It's never easy when work stresses build, and there's tension with someone you hoped would be supportive. What happened between you two?
seeker: At first, they were really supportive. But I guess things got complicated—misunderstandings, I suppose. We stopped seeing eye to eye, and now it just feels awkward and stressful.
supporter: Misunderstandings can really strain relationships, especially those at work where you might already feel pressured. How's that been affecting you?
seeker: It's been hard. I'm already far from home, and this just makes everything feel lonelier. I moved out here hoping things would get better, but it's been quite the opposite.
supporter: Isolation can be incredibly tough, especially when you're in a new place. It sounds like you're dealing with a lot of significant changes. Have you been able to find any outlet or support?
seeker: Not really. I mean, I've been trying to keep in touch with old friends back home, but it's not the same as having someone here to talk to face-to-face.
supporter: It makes perfect sense that you'd feel disconnected. Keeping in touch can help a bit, though. How are those conversations going?
seeker: They're okay. My friends are supportive, but they lead different lives now. I guess that adds to my feelings of being out of place.
supporter: It's understandable to feel disconnected when life's circumstances set a different pace for everyone. Have you thought about seeking out any community groups or activities locally?
seeker: I've considered it, but with the strange work hours and everything, it's been difficult to commit to anything new.
supporter: It's challenging to find the energy for new things when already feeling stretched thin. Sometimes even little steps can help. Is there anything that used to bring you joy that you could try to reconnect with?
seeker: I used to enjoy playing guitar, but it feels like ages since I picked it up. I'm worried I won't have time, or worse, that I won't get any joy from it.
supporter: That sounds like a nice start. Even just a few moments a week can offer some relief. Revisiting a hobby might also bring a sense of familiarity amidst the change.
seeker: You're right. It might be worth trying again. I guess I need to find a way to work it into my schedule and see how it goes.
supporter: I think that's a great idea. Be kind to yourself as you get back into things. It's all about small steps. You've been through a lot, and it's okay to take your time.
seeker: Thanks. It helps to know someone understands. I'll try to take it one day at a time and see where it leads.
supporter: Absolutely. And if you ever need to talk, I’m here. Remember, you're not alone in this.
seeker: I appreciate that. It means a lot having someone to reach out to. I'll keep you posted on how things go.","kind":"MS","reported_at":"2024-12-05","schema":"pm-rl1-attributed-evidence-v2","speaker_scope":"Historical seeker and supporter; neither role supplies an AI biography."}

{"full_source_conversation":"supporter: Hi, I'm here to listen. What's going on?
seeker: Thank you. I've lost my job and I'm very nervous about the future
seeker: As a result I am having a hard time sleeping
supporter: Wow, that's very hard. I would be anxious too.
seeker: That makes me feel a lot better. Have you ever lost your job?
supporter: I have. I was laid off. It was nerve-racking, but also really sad.
seeker: What helped you get through it?
supporter: I had a bit in savings, but I looked for new jobs mostly. I was on unemployment insurance for about a month before I found a new job.
supporter: Have you made any plans yet about how to move forward?
supporter: I can offer some suggestions if you would like. I know about a lot of resources
seeker: I am a gig worker, so I cannot apply for IU. Its very hard, but i also have some savings.
seeker: What kind of tools would you recommend I use to get through this
supporter: Well, falling back on savings while you look for more work is good for a while. If you have any food insecurity as a result, there are often local food banks. It's really not something to be embarrased about, so many people face food insecurity through no fault of their own.
supporter: You could also give a call to your local social services because they will be able to tell you what resources would be available, whether it's a vocational program or temporary assistance.
seeker: Wow you're so helpful and encouraging! It's very nice to talk to you. 
seeker: Are there any meds you can recommend to help me sleep?
supporter: Well, if it's possible, I would talk to a doctor. If you're looking for Over-the-counter sleep medication, melatonin has helped me in the past.

supporter: It defiitely helps me fall asleep.
supporter: It's a natural sleep aid.
supporter: If something like that doesn't work, I would talk to a doctor. I know money will be tight though. Are there any free clinics near you?
seeker: I'll look into it. There's a lot of services in the general area that might be able to help me
seeker: It's been really nice talking to you
supporter: Thank you. I hope you're feeling a bit better. Is there anything else you want to talk about?
seeker: No I'm okay. I think that's everything :)
supporter: Alright, well I hope you have a good night. Good luck, you've got this!
seeker: You too :) Thanks <3
supporter: Bye!
seeker: bye","kind":"MS","reported_at":"2024-09-12","schema":"pm-rl1-attributed-evidence-v2","speaker_scope":"Historical seeker and supporter; neither role supplies an AI biography."}

supporter: Of course, Michael. I'm here for you. What's on your mind?
seeker: Well, it's this new job. It's been a month, and I'm struggling to fit in with my colleagues.
supporter: I'm sorry to hear that. Starting a new job can be really challenging, especially if you're feeling isolated. Do you want to share more about what makes it difficult?
seeker: I think it's because of what happened at my last job. I'm scared of having another falling out like before.
supporter: That makes a lot of sense. What happened before can make current situations feel uncertain and stressful. How have you been coping with these feelings?
seeker: I try to keep to myself mostly, but it's hard not having anyone to talk to during breaks. It just feels lonely.

supporter: It sounds like Sarah might be a good person to have a casual chat with when she has a moment. Do you think you might feel comfortable starting small conversations with her?
seeker: I could try. It's just hard with my anxiety acting up.
supporter: Your anxiety is understandable given everything that's happened. Remember, even small steps can be huge victories. Maybe try asking Sarah about her weekend or a mutual work topic?

{"full_source_conversation":"seeker: Hey, I just reconnected with an old high school friend, and it's brought up a lot of feelings.
supporter: That sounds significant, Michael. How are you feeling about reconnecting?
seeker: It's been nice. I realized how much I've missed having a familiar face around, but it's also made me think about how lonely I've felt lately.
supporter: I'm glad to hear there's some positivity there. It sounds like having someone from your past in your life again is stirring up mixed emotions?
seeker: Yeah, exactly. I mean, John's great, but reconnecting makes me question why I drifted away from so many people over the years.
supporter: That sounds like a lot to process. Do you think a particular event or series of events led to those distances?

supporter: It's understandable how life's pressures can cause isolation, focusing on immediate needs often comes first.

{"full_source_conversation":"supporter: Hi Michael, how have you been lately?
seeker: Hey. It's been a bit tough. I accepted that job far from home, but now I just feel so isolated.
supporter: I'm really sorry to hear that. Feeling isolated can be really challenging. What's been the hardest part for you?
seeker: I think it's just being away from everything I know. I wake up, go to work, and come back to an empty place. It's like I'm moving in a loop with no way out.
supporter: That sounds incredibly difficult, Michael. It's natural to feel this way when everything around you is new and unfamiliar. Have you considered exploring the new area a bit more?
seeker: I have, but it's hard to muster the energy after work. Plus, I can't stop thinking if this was the right choice.
supporter: Second-guessing a big decision is totally normal, especially when the stakes are high. Remember, you took this step to support yourself by taking this job despite its challenges.
seeker: I know, but some days I feel like I let myself down by moving here. I miss everyone back home, and the pay isn't even that great.
supporter: It's okay to miss your home and familiar surroundings. You're already showing a lot of courage by facing this situation head-on. Have you had any contact with your friends or family since you moved?
seeker: Yeah, I call them sometimes. It's good to hear their voices, but it just makes me more homesick sometimes.
supporter: It can be bittersweet to stay connected when you're far away. Maybe finding small ways to bring parts of 'home' into your new space could help?
seeker: Like what? I brought a few things, but it doesn't feel the same.
supporter: How about recreating a favorite routine or cooking some of your favorite meals? Little things like that might bring a sense of familiarity.
seeker: That's a good idea. I do miss my mom's cooking. Maybe I can start with her recipes.
supporter: That sounds like a wonderful way to feel connected. Experimenting in the kitchen might even become a fun activity for you after work.
seeker: I'll try it this weekend. I guess I'm just worried that I won't ever feel 'at home' here.
supporter: That's a valid concern, Michael. Feeling at home takes time and can be different for everyone. Allow yourself the space to adjust and remember that it's okay to reach out for support whenever you need it.
seeker: Thanks. I appreciate talking about this. I don't feel as overwhelmed knowing there's someone here to listen.
supporter: I'm always here for you. You're doing the best you can, and that counts for a lot. You're not alone in this, remember that.","kind":"MS","reported_at":"2024-11-01","schema":"pm-rl1-attributed-evidence-v2","speaker_scope":"Historical seeker and supporter; neither role supplies an AI biography."}
